title: R cookbook
text:
Preface
This book is an introduction to R for biologists. You don’t need any coding experience to follow it.

title: R cookbook
text:
What you will learn
We start at the very beginning, with installing R and RStudio, and work our way up to analysing and plotting real data:

Getting started: install R and RStudio, find your way around RStudio, and set up a project folder for your work.
Documenting your code: write comments and notes, so that you (and others) still understand your analysis months later.
First steps in R: store values, use functions, download the example data, read it into R, combine tables and save the result, then install packages and read an Excel file.
Data objects: the building blocks of R, such as vectors, data frames and factors.
Working with the tidyverse: filter, sort, change and summarize tables, step by step.
Control structures: repeat tasks with loops and make decisions with if-else.
Plotting your data: quick plots in base R, and figures for reports and papers with ggplot2.
Statistics in R: summary statistics, linear models, t-tests and ANOVAs, and how to check their assumptions. Note: This chapter is still work in progress
Working with annotation data: handle a large table from a genome annotation and turn it into a heatmap. Note: This chapter is still work in progress

The first chapters build on each other, so work through them in order. Later on, you can also come back to single chapters and use them as a reference.

title: R cookbook
text:
Base R and the tidyverse
There are two common styles of writing R code. Base R uses the functions that come with R itself. The tidyverse is a collection of packages that lets you build an analysis from small steps that each do one job. In the first chapters you learn base R, because you will meet it everywhere: in older scripts, in other people’s code and in help pages. From the chapter “Working with the tidyverse” on, we switch to the tidyverse, because it is easier to read and to change. That chapter also explains the difference in more detail.

title: R cookbook
text:
The example data
Most chapters use data from a real plant experiment (Garrido-Oter et al. 2018). Arabidopsis thaliana plants were grown with little or plenty of phosphate, an important plant nutrient, and with or without root bacteria. We then measured how long their roots grew and how heavy their shoots got. Working with real data means that you will also meet the things that make real data messy, such as missing values and groups of different sizes. In the chapter “First steps in R” you learn how to download the data.

title: R cookbook
text:
How to use this book

Type the code yourself. Copying and pasting works, but typing helps you remember, and your typos teach you how to read error messages.
Work in a Quarto document. From the first chapter on, you write your code in a Quarto document in RStudio. Between the code, write down what you did, what you see in the results and which questions you have. These notes become your own reference.
Do the exercises. Most chapters have short exercises. The solutions are hidden: try it yourself first, and only then click on “Solution”.
Don’t worry about errors. Everyone gets them, all the time. Read the message, check your spelling and brackets, and try again.

title: R cookbook
text:
Further reading
Two separate tutorials go deeper into topics of this book. They use a different data set, measurements of penguins, which is good practice for using the same functions on new data:

An introduction into the tidyverse
An introduction into ggplot





Garrido-Oter, Ruben, Ryohei Thomas Nakano, Nina Dombrowski, Ka-Wai Ma, Alice C. McHardy, and Paul Schulze-Lefert. 2018. “Modular Traits of the Rhizobiales Root Microbiota and Their Evolutionary Relationship with Symbiotic Rhizobia.” Cell Host & Microbe 24 (1): 155–167.e5. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2018.06.006.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.1 Installation
R is a free, open source programming language for statistics and data analysis. It is widely used in biology, for example to analyse experiments, run statistical tests and make plots.
This chapter gets you set up. You will install R and RStudio, learn your way around RStudio, make a project folder for this tutorial and write your first Quarto document. In the chapter Documenting your code you learn how to write good notes in your Quarto document, and in First steps in R you start working with real data.
To follow this tutorial you need two programs: R and RStudio. R is the program that actually runs your code. RStudio is an editor that makes working with R easier: you write your code in it, run it, and see your tables and plots in one window. RStudio needs R to work, so install R first.
Both programs are free and work on Windows, Mac and Linux.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.1.1 Step 1: Install R

Go to the R download page: https://cran.r-project.org/
Click the download link for your operating system.

Windows: click “Download R for Windows”, then “base”, then the download link at the top of the page.
Mac: click “Download R for macOS”. There are two installers. Pick the one that matches the chip in your Mac: “arm64” for newer Macs with an Apple chip (M1, M2, …) and “x86_64” for older Macs with an Intel chip. If you are not sure, click the Apple menu and choose “About This Mac”.

Open the file you downloaded and follow the steps of the installer. The default settings are fine.



1.1.2 Step 2: Install RStudio

Go to the RStudio download page: https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/
R is already installed, so you can skip step 1 on that page. Download the RStudio installer for your operating system.
Open the file you downloaded and follow the steps of the installer.



1.1.3 Step 3: Check that it works
Open RStudio. You do not need to open R itself, RStudio starts it for you. In the window called Console (by default on the left side) you should see a message that starts with the R version, for example R version 4.4.2.
Click into the Console, type the following and press Enter:

1 + 1

[1] 2


If R answers with [1] 2, everything is installed correctly. The [1] just means that this is the first value of the answer.






Note



If you already have R and RStudio installed, check how old they are. Packages are often only built for recent R versions, so a very old R can cause errors when you install packages. To see your R version, type R.version.string in the Console.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.2 Find your way around RStudio
R on its own only has a command line: you type a command, press Enter and get an answer. RStudio puts a graphical interface around R, with windows and buttons, so that you can see your code, your data and your plots side by side.

1.2.1 The four panes
RStudio is split into four areas, called panes:




Source (top left): this is where you write and edit your files, for example the Quarto document you create below. This pane only appears once you open or create a file.
Console (bottom left): this is where R actually runs your code and prints the results. You can also type commands here directly.
Environment (top right): lists everything you have stored in R during this session, for example tables you have read in. Click on a table to look at it.
Files, Plots, Packages, Help (bottom right): shows the files in your folder, your plots, the packages you have installed and the help pages.

You can rearrange the panes under Tools > Global Options > Pane Layout, so the positions on your computer might be different.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.3 Make a project folder
Before you write any code, make a folder for this tutorial. R needs to know where your files are, and a clear folder structure makes this easy.

1.3.1 The working directory
R always works from one folder on your computer, the working directory. When you tell R to read a file, for example data/Growth_Data.txt, it looks for it starting from the working directory. To see which folder R is currently using, type:

getwd()

It is a good idea to make one folder per project, with the same structure each time: for example a subfolder for the input data, one for the output files, and your scripts. Here is an example for a project folder that contains four sub-projects:



In the example above you can see that I have different sub-folders for different analyses I did for a project of mine. One sub-folder is open and you see that it contains an R script and folders for the input and output files. If you plan to share your analysis with others, it is also good to add a README file that explains what the analysis is about.


1.3.2 Make an RStudio project
The easiest way to get the working directory right is an RStudio Project. A project is a folder on your computer that RStudio remembers. When you open the project, RStudio automatically sets the working directory to that folder. This means you never have to type the full path to your files, and your code keeps working if you move the folder or share it with someone else.
To create a project for this tutorial:

Go to File > New Project > New Directory > New Project.
Give the folder a name, for example R_tutorial, and choose where it should be saved with “Browse”.
Click “Create Project”.

RStudio now opens the project. You will see a file ending in .Rproj in the Files pane. The next time you want to work on this tutorial, open RStudio and use File > Open Project, or double-click the .Rproj file.
You can check that it worked with getwd(). It should print the path of your new project folder.
From now on, all paths in this tutorial are written relative to the project folder. For example, data/Growth_Data.txt means “the file Growth_Data.txt in the folder data inside my project folder”.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.4 Write your first Quarto document

1.4.1 Console or document?
You can type code directly into the Console, but once you close RStudio that code is gone. Also, if you want to repeat an analysis a few weeks later, you will not remember exactly what you typed.
That is why you should keep your work in a file. In this tutorial we use a Quarto document, a file that ends in .qmd. A Quarto document holds two things: your R code, and normal text around it. The code is a record of everything you did, and you can run it again at any time. The text is where you write down what you are doing and why, what you notice in the results, and which questions you still have. When you come back to your analysis later, or discuss it with your supervisor, these notes are often as useful as the code itself.
Some rules of thumb:

Use the Console for quick checks that you do not need to keep, for example looking at a table with head().
Use your Quarto document for everything that is part of your analysis, and for your thoughts about it.



1.4.2 Create and save a Quarto document

Make sure your project is open. Its name is shown in the top right corner of RStudio.
Go to File > New File > Quarto Document. A window opens. Type a title, for example “My first analysis”, and click “Create Empty Document” at the bottom left.
Save the document with File > Save (or Ctrl+S on Windows, Cmd+S on Mac). Give it a name that ends with .qmd, for example analysis.qmd. Save it directly in your project folder, not in a subfolder (see the tip below).

RStudio can show a Quarto document in two ways, which you can switch between with the buttons Source and Visual at the top left of the document. In this tutorial we use Source, because it shows exactly what is in the file.






Tip



When you run code in a Quarto document, RStudio uses the folder where the .qmd file is saved as the working directory. If your document is in the project folder, a path like data/Growth_Data.txt works as expected. If you save it in a subfolder, R looks for data/ inside that subfolder and cannot find your files.
You can see this setting under Tools > Global Options > R Markdown, next to “Evaluate chunks in directory”. The default is “Document”. Leave it like that and save your Quarto document in the project folder.







1.4.3 Text and code chunks
A Quarto document has three parts:

A header at the top, between two lines of ---. It holds settings such as the title. You can leave it as it is for now.
Text, which you type as in any text file. R ignores it.
Code chunks: blocks of R code. A chunk starts with ```{r} and ends with ```. R only runs what is inside a chunk.

To add a chunk, click Code > Insert Chunk, or press Ctrl+Alt+I (Cmd+Option+I on Mac).
Type the following into your document below the header:
---
title: "My first analysis"
---

## Trying out R

I want to check that R can do simple maths.

```{r}
1 + 1
```

R gives 2, as expected. I am not sure yet what the [1] in front of the answer means.
The line starting with ## is a heading. You will learn more ways to format your text in the chapter Documenting your code.


1.4.4 Run a chunk
There are several ways to run your code:

Click the green arrow in the top right corner of a chunk to run the whole chunk.
Put the cursor on a line inside a chunk and press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on Mac) to run only that line.
Select several lines with the mouse and press Ctrl+Enter (Cmd+Enter on Mac) to run just those lines.




The result appears directly below the chunk. Add your thoughts about it as text below the chunk, then add the next chunk. Step by step, your document becomes a record of your analysis.






Note



At the top of the document you will also see a Render button. It turns your whole document into a report, for example an HTML page. You do not need it yet. We come back to it in the chapter Documenting your code.




1.4.5 Reading the Console
Even when you work in a Quarto document, your code is run in the Console. The symbol at the start of the last line in the Console tells you what R is doing:

> means R is ready and waits for your next command.
+ means R thinks your command is not finished yet and waits for the rest. This usually happens when you forgot a closing bracket ) or quote ". Either type the missing part, or press Esc to cancel the command and start again.

If R prints a message starting with Error, your command did not work. Read the message, it often tells you what went wrong (for example a misspelled name or a file that cannot be found). Messages starting with Warning mean the command did run, but R wants to tell you about something that might be a problem.


1.4.6 What about R scripts?
You will also come across R scripts: plain text files that end in .R and contain only code (File > New File > R Script). In a script, any notes have to be written as comments after a # sign. Scripts are useful when you run R without RStudio, for example on a computer cluster (see the optional section at the end of this chapter). For this tutorial, use your Quarto document.

title: 1  Getting started
text:
1.5 Getting help
Inside R, you can open the help page of any function by typing ? followed by the name of the function. For example, for the function mean(), which calculates an average:

?mean

The help page opens in the Help pane. In the chapter First steps in R you will learn how to read these pages.
Outside of R, good places to look for help are:

An internet search with your error message. Copy the message exactly. Very often someone has had the same problem before.
Stack Overflow, a question and answer website for programming.
The R project website, with manuals and links.

section: 1.6 Optional: start R from the terminal
text:
1.6 Optional: start R from the terminal






NoteClick to expand





You do not need this for the tutorial. It is useful if you later work on a computer cluster, where there is no RStudio.
On Linux and Mac, you can also start R directly from the terminal. Open a terminal, go to your project folder with cd and type R. You should then see something like this:



To start R, type the following in your terminal (this is a terminal command, not R code):

# start R
R

Once R has started, the terminal shows the R prompt >. Now you are inside R and can type R code. For example, to check your R version and then quit R again:

# ask what R version we have
R.version

# exit R and go back to the terminal
q()

On Windows, typing R in PowerShell does not start R, because r already means something else there. On Windows it is easiest to work in RStudio.

title: 2  Documenting your code
text:
2.1 Markdown
Code that works today can be a mystery in six months, even to the person who wrote it. Good documentation means that you, your supervisor or a colleague can later understand what you did, why you did it, and run it again to get the same result.
In the chapter Getting started, you wrote your first Quarto document, with your code in chunks and your notes in between. Before you write more code, this chapter shows how to get the most out of it:
The text in a Quarto document is written in Markdown. Markdown is a simple way to format plain text. You type a few special characters, and a program turns them into formatted text. Some examples:
Leave an empty line before a heading and before a list. Otherwise Markdown may not recognise them.
Why use Markdown instead of a word processor?
This tutorial does not cover Markdown in detail, but there is good material online:

It is used in many places, for example on GitHub, in Jupyter notebooks and in Quarto. This book itself is written in Markdown.

title: 2  Documenting your code
section: 2.2 What to write between your chunks
text:
2.2 What to write between your chunks
The text between your chunks is where your analysis becomes understandable. A few questions can help you decide what to write:

What do I do here, and why? For example: “I remove the plants without a root length measurement, because they cannot be used for the comparison.”
What do I see? Describe the result in your own words, even if it seems obvious. It might not be so obvious anymore after a few months. For example: “The table has 594 rows, one per plant.”
What surprises me? Unexpected values, odd groups, numbers that are much larger or smaller than you thought.
What questions do I have? Things you want to check later, or ask your supervisor. Writing them down while you work means you don’t forget them.

Here is an example of how this can look. It uses the growth data that you will download and read in the chapter First steps in R, so don’t worry if you don’t understand the code yet. Look at the text around it:
## Read the growth data

We read in the measurements of the plant experiment.

```{r}
growth_data <- read.table("data/Growth_Data.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE, quote = "")
head(growth_data)
dim(growth_data)
```

The table has one row per plant and 594 plants in total. The columns are the phosphate level, the bacterial treatment, the experiment, the root
length and the shoot weight.

Questions:

- Some values are `NA`. How many are there, and are they in one group?
- Why are there three experiments? Were they done at different times?
Your notes don’t need to be polished. They are mainly for you and the people you work with. Short, honest notes are much more useful than none.

title: 2  Documenting your code
text:
2.3 Comments in your code
Inside a chunk, you can write comments. Everything on a line after a # is a comment. R ignores it, so you can write anything you like there:

# this whole line is a comment
1 + 1 # a comment can also follow some code

[1] 2


Use the text between chunks for longer notes, and comments for short notes about a single line of code. Good comments explain why you do something, not only what the code does. The code already shows what happens; the reason is often the part you forget.

# not very helpful: says the same as the code
# divide 15.2 by 1000
15.2 / 1000

[1] 0.0152

# more helpful: explains why
# convert the shoot weight of 15.2 mg to g, because the other study reports g
15.2 / 1000

[1] 0.0152








Tip



In RStudio, you can turn several lines into comments at once: select them and press Ctrl+Shift+C (Cmd+Shift+C on Mac). Press it again to remove the # signs.








Note



In an R script (a .R file), comments are the only place for notes. There, it helps to start the script with a few comment lines that say who wrote it, when, and what it is for:

# Analysis of root length in the growth experiment
# Author: your name
# Date: 2026-10-19
# Purpose: test whether the bacterial strains change root length under low phosphorus

In a Quarto document, the header at the top does this job (see below).

title: 2  Documenting your code
section: 2.4 Turn your document into a report
text:
2.4 Turn your document into a report
You already know the three parts of a Quarto document from the first chapter: the header, the text and the code chunks. Here we look at the header in more detail and at how to make a report from your document.

2.4.1 The header
The header at the top of the document, between the two lines of ---, holds the settings of your document. It is a good place to say who wrote the document, when, and what it is about:
---
title: "Root length in the growth experiment"
author: "Your name"
date: "2026-10-19"
format: html
---
format: html tells Quarto to make an HTML page, which you can open in any web browser. Other formats are possible, for example pdf or docx (a Word file), but they may need extra software.


2.4.2 Render your document
To create a report, click the Render button at the top of the document. Quarto then runs all code from top to bottom in a fresh R session and puts the text, the code and its results (tables, plots) together. The report is saved next to your .qmd file, here as an HTML file with the same name. RStudio usually also opens it for you.






Tip



Because rendering starts from a fresh R session, it only works if your document contains every step: loading packages, reading the data, and so on. If it renders without errors, you know that your analysis does not secretly depend on something you once typed into the Console.


If rendering fails, Quarto prints an error message in the Background Jobs tab next to the Console. It tells you in which chunk the problem is.  Fix the chunk, run it on its own to check, and render again.


2.4.3 Chunk options
You can control what a chunk does and what appears in the report with chunk options. In Quarto, you write them at the top of the chunk, on lines starting with #|:
```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

head(growth_data)
```
Some useful options:

echo: false hides the code, but shows its results in the report. Useful for plots.
eval: false shows the code, but does not run it.
include: false runs the code, but shows neither the code nor its results. The results can still be used by later chunks.
warning: false hides warnings in the report.
message: false hides messages, for example the ones some packages print when you load them.
fig-cap: "..." adds a caption to a plot.

You find all options on the Quarto website.


2.4.4 Optional: using languages other than R






NoteClick to expand





You do not need this for the tutorial.
Quarto documents can also contain code in other languages, such as bash (the language of the Linux and Mac command line) or Python. You only change the name in the curly brackets at the top of the chunk, for example ```{bash} instead of ```{r}.
This is useful if part of your analysis runs on the command line, for example on a computer cluster, and another part in R. You can document both steps in the same file.
Some examples with bash:

The last two examples use the data folder and the growth data, which you download in the chapter First steps in R.
To run bash chunks, bash must be installed on your computer. On Mac and Linux it already is. On Windows, it is available for example through Git for Windows or WSL. If you don’t have bash, these chunks give an error, but this does not affect your R chunks.
A general introduction into bash and awk is provided in a separate tutorial on GitHub.

title: 2  Documenting your code
text:
2.5 Good practices
These practices are useful in any programming language. You don’t need to follow all of them from day one, but the earlier they become habits, the easier your life will be. Some of them mention things that you only learn in the next chapters, such as packages or saving tables. Use this list as a checklist and come back to it later.

Keep each project in its own folder, with subfolders for input data and output files, and use an RStudio project (see Getting started).
Fill in the header of your document: who wrote it, when, and what it is about.
Load all packages at the top of your document, so you see at once what it needs.
Write down what you see and what you wonder about between your chunks, not only the code.
Comment your code so that you can still understand it in 5 years. Explain why, not only what.
Use descriptive names for objects: short, but clear enough that you know what is inside, for example growth_data instead of df1.
Break your code into small steps and check the result of each step, for example with head() and dim(). One line per step is easier to read and to fix than one long line that does everything.
Render your document from time to time. This checks that it still runs from top to bottom without errors.
Never change your raw data by hand. Read it into R, change it there, and save the result in a new file. Then your document records every change.
Save tables, not workspaces. Write the tables you need with write.table() instead of saving the whole workspace. The workspace hides how the objects were made; your document and the tables don’t.
If you use random numbers, for example for sampling, set and report the starting point with set.seed(), for example set.seed(42). Then you get the same random numbers each time you run the code.
Record the software versions you used. Packages change over time, and the same code can give different results or errors with another version. The function sessionInfo() prints your R version and all loaded packages with their versions. Run it at the end of your document:
