title: 3  First steps in R
text:
3.1 Store values with <-
In this chapter you write your first R code. We start with the basics: how to store a value and how to use a function. Then we download the example data, read it into R, look at it, combine it with a second table and save the result in a new file. At the end, we install our first package and use it to read an Excel file.
Before you start, open the RStudio project you made in the chapter Getting started and create a new Quarto document for this chapter, for example first_steps.qmd. Save it directly in your project folder. Type the code of this chapter into chunks in that document and run it from there. Between the chunks, write down what you did, what you see in the results and which questions you have, as described in the chapter Documenting your code.
In the chapter Getting started, you used R as a calculator: you typed 1 + 1 and R printed 2. But R did not keep the result. To use a result again later, for example a table you read in, you need to store it under a name. For this, R uses the <- symbol. The name and the value together are called an object (some people also say variable). Once a value is stored, you can use the name instead of the value:
# store some numbers
x <- 1
y <- 4

# do some simple math with the numbers we have stored
x + y

[1] 5
You can read x <- 1 as “x gets the value 1”. In RStudio, the keyboard shortcut Alt + - (Option + - on Mac) types the <- for you.
Some general rules:
Every object you create appears in the Environment pane (top right in RStudio).

title: 3  First steps in R
text:
R is case sensitive: x and X are two different objects.
If an object with that name already exists, R overwrites it without asking.
Text (R calls it a character value) needs quotes around it, for example "hello". Without quotes, R thinks hello is the name of an object and looks for it.
Names can contain letters, numbers, _ and ., but cannot start with a number. Choose names that are short but tell you what is inside, for example growth_data instead of df1.

title: 3  First steps in R
text:
3.2 Functions
A function is a piece of code that does one specific job, for example calculating a mean or reading a table. R comes with many functions already built in, and packages (see below) add many more.
You use a function by writing its name followed by round brackets. Inside the brackets you put the input for the function:

# print something to the screen
print(3 + 5)

[1] 8

# calculate the natural logarithm of 10
log(10)

[1] 2.302585



3.2.1 How to write arguments
The values inside the brackets are called arguments. They tell the function what to work on and how exactly to behave. Arguments are separated by commas, and you write them as name = value. For example, round() rounds a number, and its argument digits says how many decimals you want to keep:

# round to 2 decimals
round(3.14159, digits = 2)

[1] 3.14


You can often leave out the name of an argument. R then matches the values by their position, so this gives the same result:

# same as above, without the argument name
round(3.14159, 2)

[1] 3.14


If you don’t set an argument at all, R uses its default value. For round(), the default is digits = 0, so you get a whole number:

round(3.14159)

[1] 3


Writing out the names makes your code easier to read, especially for functions with many arguments. You will see this a lot below, for example in read.table("data/Growth_Data.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE).


3.2.2 Find out what a function does
How do you know which arguments a function has, and what their defaults are? The help page tells you. Type ? followed by the function name:

?round

The help page opens in the Help pane. Most help pages have the same parts:

Description: what the function does.
Usage: how to call the function. Here you see all arguments, and for each argument with a default you see that default, for example round(x, digits = 0).
Arguments: what each argument means.
Examples: at the very bottom. You can copy these into your document to try them out.

Help pages are written for people who already know some R, so they can be hard to read at first. It is fine to only look at Usage and Examples in the beginning.

title: 3  First steps in R
section: 3.3 Look at and clean up your workspace
text:
3.3 Look at and clean up your workspace
Everything you have stored during your current R session is called your workspace. You see it in the Environment pane, but you can also list it with ls():

# list the objects in the current workspace
ls()

[1] "x" "y"


To remove an object, use rm():

# remove the object x
rm(x)

# x is gone, only y is left
ls()

[1] "y"


To remove everything at once, use rm(list = ls()). This combines two functions: ls() makes a list of all objects, and the argument list of rm() tells it to remove everything in that list. This is useful when you want to run your document again from a clean start.






Tip



When you close RStudio, it may ask whether you want to save your workspace to a file called .RData. Answer No. If you say yes, all your objects are loaded again the next time you open the project, and it becomes hard to tell whether your document still works on its own. Your document is the record of your analysis, not the workspace. You can switch the question off under Tools > Global Options > General: untick “Restore .RData into workspace at startup” and set “Save workspace to .RData on exit” to “Never”.

title: 3  First steps in R
text:
3.4 Get the data

3.4.1 The example data
In the next chapters we work with data from a real plant experiment, published in Garrido-Oter et al. (2018). We grew Arabidopsis thaliana plants with or without root bacteria and wanted to know whether the bacteria help the plant grow when it does not get enough phosphate, an important plant nutrient. The plants were grown with either a low (50 µM) or a high (625 µM) amount of phosphate. They were either inoculated with one of two Rhizobium strains (129E or 13C) or were mock-treated, i.e. treated in the same way but without bacteria (mock). The mock plants are our control.
There are two data files:
Growth_Data.txt contains the root length (Rootlength, in mm) and the shoot fresh weight (FW_shoot_mg, in mg) of each plant. The column Nutrient says whether the plant got low (low_P) or high (high_P) phosphate, and Condition says whether it was treated with a strain or was a mock control. The column Experiment tells you in which of the 3 repeats of the experiment (ex61, ex64, ex65) the plant was measured. The published data contains more experiments, but we only use the three in which all treatments were measured. For a few plants, the root length or the shoot weight could not be measured, so this file has some empty cells.
Timecourse.txt follows up on this. Strain 129E helped the plants grow, so we wanted to know how long it takes until the effect appears. We measured the root length of plants with and without 129E at 6 time points: 0, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 18 days after transfer to the treatment (Timepoint).
Both files were made from the raw data table that was published with the paper. This table is an Excel file with one sheet per figure (mmc5.xlsx). We download it as well, to practise reading Excel files.


3.4.2 Download the files
The example data for this tutorial is stored on GitHub, a website for sharing code and files. You can download it directly with R, so you do not need a GitHub account.
Make sure you have your project open and run the code below. It uses a few new functions:

dir.create() makes a new folder in your project. We make two: data for the input files and output_examples for files we will write later.
download.file() downloads a file from a web address (url) and saves it under the name you give it (destfile).
mode = "wb" tells R to copy the file exactly as it is. Without it, R on Windows changes the line endings of text files, and the file is no longer identical to the original. Excel files can even become unreadable.

We only want to create a folder or download a file if we don’t have it yet. Otherwise, every time you run your document again, R would download the files again and overwrite the ones you already have. To do this, we put each step inside an if:

dir.exists() and file.exists() check whether a folder or file is already there. They answer TRUE or FALSE.
The ! in front means “not”. It turns TRUE into FALSE and the other way around.
if (...) { ... } only runs the code between the curly brackets { } if the part in the round brackets ( ) is TRUE.

So if (!file.exists("data/Growth_Data.txt")) { ... } reads as: “if the file data/Growth_Data.txt does not exist, run the code inside the brackets”. You will learn more about if in the chapter on control structures.

# make a folder for the input data, but only if it does not exist yet
if (!dir.exists("data")) {
  dir.create("data")
}

# make a folder for our output files, but only if it does not exist yet
if (!dir.exists("output_examples")) {
  dir.create("output_examples")
}

# download the growth data, but only if we don't have it yet
if (!file.exists("data/Growth_Data.txt")) {
  download.file(url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/R_cookbook/main/data/Growth_Data.txt",
                destfile = "data/Growth_Data.txt",
                mode = "wb")
}

# download the timecourse data, but only if we don't have it yet
if (!file.exists("data/Timecourse.txt")) {
  download.file(url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/R_cookbook/main/data/Timecourse.txt",
                destfile = "data/Timecourse.txt",
                mode = "wb")
}

# download the Excel file with the raw data of the paper, but only if we don't have it yet
if (!file.exists("data/mmc5.xlsx")) {
  download.file(url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/R_cookbook/main/data/mmc5.xlsx",
                destfile = "data/mmc5.xlsx",
                mode = "wb")
}

The first time you run this, R prints a few lines for each download, ending with a line that starts with downloaded. If you run it again, nothing happens, because the files are already there.






Tip



If you ever want a fresh copy of a file, for example because you changed it by accident, delete it in the Files pane and run the code again.


Now check that the download worked. file.exists() answers TRUE if a file is there, and file.size() gives its size in bytes. Your numbers should be the same as below.

# are the files there?
file.exists("data/Growth_Data.txt")

[1] TRUE

file.exists("data/Timecourse.txt")

[1] TRUE

file.exists("data/mmc5.xlsx")

[1] TRUE

# how large are they (in bytes)?
file.size("data/Growth_Data.txt")

[1] 15811

file.size("data/Timecourse.txt")

[1] 46050

file.size("data/mmc5.xlsx")

[1] 441420


If you see FALSE, look at the Files pane. Is there a data folder in your project, and is it spelled exactly like this? R is case sensitive, so Data and data are two different folders.

title: 3  First steps in R
text:
3.5 Read data into R
To work with data, we first need to read it into R. We use the function read.table() and store the result under the name growth_data. The file is not directly in our project folder but in the subfolder data, so we write data/Growth_Data.txt.

# read in the growth data
growth_data <- read.table("data/Growth_Data.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE, quote = "")

# check the first few lines of our data
head(growth_data)


  



When R reads a table, it stores it as a data frame. A data frame is R’s name for a table: each row is one measurement (here: one plant) and each column is one variable (for example the nutrient condition or the root length). Empty cells in a table become NA in R, which means “not available”, i.e. a missing value.
head() shows the first 6 rows of a table. Use it every time you read or change a table, to check that everything went alright.
The arguments we gave to read.table():

sep = the character that separates the columns. Some programs use commas, others use tabs. Our files use tabs, and a tab is written as "\t". If your data uses commas, write sep = ",". If you leave out sep, read.table() treats any whitespace (spaces and tabs) as a separator.
header = whether the first row of the file contains the column names. header = TRUE means “yes, the first row contains the column names”.
quote = which characters mark the start and end of a text. By default, R treats both " and ' this way. That causes problems as soon as a cell contains a single ', for example in a gene name like 5' nuclease: R then thinks a text starts there and reads the rest of the file as one long piece of text. You may end up with missing rows or even an empty table, and R only shows a warning, not an error. With quote = "" we tell R that no character has a special meaning, so every cell is read exactly as it is.

Also make sure that your table has no hash symbols (#) in it. By default, read.table() reads everything after a # as a comment and ignores it.






Note



In other people’s code you will often see T and F instead of TRUE and FALSE, for example header = T. R understands both. In this tutorial we write TRUE and FALSE in full, because it is easier to read.


The first rows are complete. The empty cells we mentioned in the data description are further down the table, and R shows them as NA. You will learn how to deal with such missing values in the chapter Working with the tidyverse.
A few more functions that help you check a table:

dim() gives the dimensions of a table: first the number of rows, then the number of columns.
colnames() gives the column names.
rownames() gives the row names. Usually these are just the numbers 1, 2, 3, and so on. Our table has 594 rows, so we only look at the first few with head().


# check the dimensions of our data
dim(growth_data)

[1] 594   5



# check the column names
colnames(growth_data)

[1] "Nutrient"    "Condition"   "Experiment"  "Rootlength"  "FW_shoot_mg"



# check the first few row names
head(rownames(growth_data))

[1] "1" "2" "3" "4" "5" "6"


Now read the timecourse data in the same way:

# read in the timecourse data
timecourse <- read.table("data/Timecourse.txt", sep = "\t", header = TRUE, quote = "")

# check the first few lines and the dimensions
head(timecourse)


  


dim(timecourse)

[1] 2323    4








Tip



For very large tables, read.table() can be slow. The function fread() from the package data.table is a much faster alternative.

title: 3  First steps in R
section: 3.6 Look at parts of your table
text:
3.6 Look at parts of your table
head() shows all columns of the first few rows. Often you only want to see some of the columns, or a single column. For this you need three pieces of R syntax. You will learn more about them in the chapter Data objects.

3.6.1 c() combines values
c() stands for “combine”. It puts several values together into a vector, which is a list of values of the same kind (for example only numbers, or only text):

# a vector with three numbers
c(1, 5, 10)

[1]  1  5 10

# a vector with two column names
c("Condition", "Rootlength")

[1] "Condition"  "Rootlength"




3.6.2 [rows, columns] selects part of a table
With square brackets you can select rows and columns from a data frame. The part before the comma selects rows, the part after the comma selects columns. If you leave one side empty, R takes all of them.

# rows 1 to 3, and only the columns Condition and Rootlength
growth_data[1:3, c("Condition", "Rootlength")]


  



Here 1:3 means “the numbers 1 to 3”, so rows 1, 2 and 3. If we write growth_data[, c("Condition", "Rootlength")] instead, with nothing before the comma, we get these two columns for all 594 rows.


3.6.3 $ takes one column
With $ you can take a single column from a data frame by its name:

# the first few values of the column Rootlength
head(growth_data$Rootlength)

[1] 40.4 38.0 74.7 34.4 31.9 66.5


You can also use $ together with <- to add a new column. If you give a single value, R copies it into every row. We will do this in the merge section below.

title: 3  First steps in R
section: 3.7 Find the unique combinations with unique()
text:
3.7 Find the unique combinations with unique()
unique() removes duplicates and keeps each value, or each combination of values, only once.
In our growth data, each plant got one combination of nutrient and condition, for example low_P and 129E. Many plants share the same combination. If we take the columns Nutrient and Condition and remove the duplicates, we get a short overview of all treatments in our experiment:

# make a table that lists each combination of nutrient and condition only once
mapping_file <- unique(growth_data[, c("Nutrient", "Condition")])

# view the data
mapping_file


  



Instead of 594 rows we now have 6: 2 nutrient levels times 3 conditions. A table like this, which describes each sample or treatment, is often called a mapping file or metadata.
The numbers on the left are the row names. unique() keeps the row names of the first row in which each combination appears.

title: 3  First steps in R
text:
3.8 Combine two tables with merge()
Often we have extra information about our samples in a separate table and want to add it to our data. The function merge() combines two tables based on columns they have in common. Each row in the first table gets the information from the matching row in the second table.
Let’s add a column Source to our mapping file that says from which figure of the paper the data comes. This is useful if you later combine data from several figures or experiments:

# add a new column that says where the data comes from
mapping_file$Source <- "Fig S5A,B"

# view the data
mapping_file


  



Now we merge the mapping file with our growth data:

# merge our growth data with the mapping file
new_data_frame <- merge(growth_data, mapping_file, by = c("Nutrient", "Condition"))

# view the data
head(new_data_frame)


  



The argument by says which columns to use for matching the rows. Here we need two: a row in growth_data matches a row in mapping_file only if both the nutrient and the condition are the same. Note that merge() sorts the result by the by columns, so the rows are now in a different order than in growth_data.
After a merge, always check that you have the number of rows you expected. We still want 594 rows (one per plant) and one extra column:

# compare the dimensions before and after merging
dim(growth_data)

[1] 594   5

dim(new_data_frame)

[1] 594   6








WarningA common mistake: matching on too few columns



What happens if we only match on Condition? In mapping_file, each condition appears twice, once for low_P and once for high_P. So every plant now matches two rows, and R makes a copy of the plant for each match:

# merge on Condition only (this is wrong!)
wrong_merge <- merge(growth_data, mapping_file, by = "Condition")

dim(wrong_merge)

[1] 1188    7

head(wrong_merge)


  



We suddenly have twice as many plants as before, and there is no error message. You also see two new columns, Nutrient.x and Nutrient.y. Both tables had a column called Nutrient that was not used for matching, so R keeps both. To tell them apart, R adds .x to the column from the first table and .y to the column from the second table.
If you see columns ending in .x and .y, or more rows than you expected, check the by argument.








Note



By default, merge() drops all rows that have no match in the other table. For example, if a condition is in growth_data but not in mapping_file, those plants disappear from the result without a warning. If you want to keep all rows of the first table, add all.x = TRUE. R then fills the missing values with NA:
merge(growth_data, mapping_file, by = c("Nutrient", "Condition"), all.x = TRUE)

title: 3  First steps in R
section: 3.9 Write data into a text file
text:
3.9 Write data into a text file
We changed our table, so let’s save the result in a new file. We use write.table() and save the file in the folder output_examples. As for reading, the path starts from our project folder.

write.table(new_data_frame, "output_examples/growth_data_changed.txt", sep = "\t", row.names = FALSE, quote = FALSE, na = "")

The arguments:

sep = "\t" separates the columns with tabs, the same format as our input files.
row.names = FALSE leaves out the row names. With TRUE, R writes the row numbers as an extra first column. That column has no name in the header, so the header row then has one column less than the other rows, and other programs may shift all column names by one.
quote = FALSE writes text without quotes around it.
na = "" writes missing values as empty cells, like in our input file. By default, R writes the text NA, which other programs may read as text instead of as a missing value.

You can now open growth_data_changed.txt in the Files pane or in a text editor to look at it.

title: 3  First steps in R
text:
3.10 Packages
So far we only used functions that come with R. We also downloaded an Excel file, but R cannot read Excel files on its own. For this, we need a package.
A package is a collection of extra functions (and sometimes data) that someone wrote and shared. Base R can already do a lot, but for many tasks, such as reading Excel files, nicer plots or specific statistical tests, you will use packages. Most packages are stored on CRAN, the same website where you downloaded R.
Working with a package takes two steps:

Install the package. This downloads it to your computer. You only do this once (and again when you want to update it).
Load the package with library(). This makes its functions available in your current R session. R forgets loaded packages when you close it, so you do this every time you start R. That is why library() calls belong at the top of your document.

The package for Excel files is called readxl. It is part of the tidyverse, a collection of packages that we use a lot from the chapter Working with the tidyverse on, for example for changing tables and making plots. So let’s install the whole tidyverse now. This installs all of its packages at once, including readxl, so it can take a few minutes.

# install the package (only once, type this in the Console)
install.packages("tidyverse")

# load the package (every session, put this at the top of your document)
library(tidyverse)

When you load the tidyverse, R prints a message with the packages it loaded, and a list of “conflicts”. The conflicts tell you that some tidyverse functions have the same name as functions in base R, for example filter(). From now on, R uses the tidyverse version. This is expected and nothing to worry about.
Note the quotes: install.packages() needs the name as text in quotes, while library() works without them.
Instead of typing install.packages(), you can also install packages in RStudio with the Packages tab (bottom right) and the Install button.






Note



Put install.packages() in the Console, not in your document. Otherwise R downloads the package again every time you run the document.



3.10.1 Updating packages
Packages are updated regularly. To update them:

old.packages() lists the installed packages for which a newer version exists.
update.packages() updates them. R asks you for each package whether you want to update it. With update.packages(ask = FALSE) it updates everything without asking. This can take a while if you have not done it for some time.

In RStudio, you can also use the Update button in the Packages tab.
Updates are usually a good idea, but sometimes a new version of a package works differently and older code no longer runs. This is one reason to record which package versions you used (see the chapter on documenting your code).

title: 3  First steps in R
text:
3.11 Read an Excel file
A lot of data is stored in Excel files. You could save each sheet as a text file in Excel first, but with the package readxl R can read Excel files directly. library(tidyverse) only loads the main tidyverse packages, and readxl is not one of them. So we load it ourselves:

library(readxl)

An Excel file can have several sheets. excel_sheets() lists their names:

# which sheets are in the file?
excel_sheets("data/mmc5.xlsx")

 [1] "metadata"      "Fig 3A"        "Fig 3B"        "Fig 4B PRL"   
 [5] "Fig 4B #CELLS" "Fig 5A"        "Fig 6A"        "Fig 6B"       
 [9] "Fig 7"         "Fig S4A"       "Fig S5A,B"     "Fig S5C"      
[13] "Fig S5D"       "Fig S5E"       "Fig S6C,D"     "Fig S6E"      
[17] "Fig S6F"       "Fig S6G"      


The growth data comes from the sheet Fig S5A,B. Let’s read it with read_excel(). The argument sheet says which sheet we want:

# read one sheet
growth_excel <- read_excel("data/mmc5.xlsx", sheet = "Fig S5A,B")

New names:
• `` -> `...2`
• `` -> `...3`
• `` -> `...4`
• `` -> `...5`
• `` -> `...6`

head(growth_excel)


  



This does not look right. The column names are # Raw data for Fig S5A,B, ...2, ...3 and so on, and the real column names are in the first row. If you open the file in Excel you see why: the first line of the sheet is a comment, and the table only starts in the second line. read_excel() always uses the first line as column names.
We can tell read_excel() to skip the first line with skip = 1:

# skip the comment line
growth_excel <- read_excel("data/mmc5.xlsx", sheet = "Fig S5A,B", skip = 1)

head(growth_excel)


  



Better. But there is one more problem, which is easy to miss. Underneath each column name, R shows what kind of values the column contains: <chr> means text (character) and <dbl> means numbers. The columns Primary Root Length (mm) and Shoot Fresh Weight (mg) should contain numbers, but they are <chr>. The reason is that in this sheet, missing values are written as the text NA. R does not know this is a missing value, so it reads the whole column as text, and you can’t calculate with it. With the argument na we tell R which cells mean “missing value”. We give it two options, combined with c(): an empty cell ("") and the text "NA":

# treat empty cells and the text "NA" as missing values
growth_excel <- read_excel("data/mmc5.xlsx", sheet = "Fig S5A,B", skip = 1, na = c("", "NA"))

head(growth_excel)


  



Now both measurement columns are numbers (<dbl>).
You may have noticed that the column Nutrient says 50 mM P. This is a typo in the published table: the plants got 50 µM and 625 µM phosphate. Real data contains mistakes like this, and it is one more reason to always look at your data after reading it.
A few more things to notice:

read_excel() gives you a tibble. A tibble is a data frame with a slightly different way of printing, for example with the column types shown under the names. Everything you learn about data frames also works on tibbles.
The column names contain spaces and brackets, for example Primary Root Length (mm). R can handle them, but you have to put backticks around such names when you use them, for example growth_excel$`Primary Root Length (mm)`. This is one reason why short names without spaces are easier to work with.

This is how we made Growth_Data.txt: we read the sheet as shown here, gave the columns shorter names, kept only the three experiments in which all treatments were measured and saved the table with write.table(), just as you did above. You can find the full script, make_example_data.R, on GitHub.






Tip



When you collect your own data in Excel, you make your life in R much easier if you:

start the table in the first row, without titles or comments above it
use short column names without spaces or special characters
leave cells empty when a value is missing, and don’t write text such as NA, - or missing in number columns
use one sheet per table

title: 3  First steps in R
text:
3.12 Summary
In this chapter you learned how to:

store values in objects with <-
use functions and set their arguments, and look up a function with ?
list and remove objects with ls() and rm()
download files with download.file()
read a table with read.table() and check it with head(), dim() and colnames()
select rows and columns with [ , ] and a single column with $
remove duplicates with unique() and combine tables with merge()
save a table with write.table()
install packages once with install.packages() and load them in every session with library()
read a sheet of an Excel file with read_excel(), and use skip and na to deal with untidy sheets


3.12.1 Exercise
Use the timecourse data frame for these questions:

How many rows and columns does it have?
Which time points were measured? Hint: use unique() on the column Timepoint.
Make a table that lists each combination of Nutrient, Condition and Timepoint only once. How many rows does it have?







TipSolution






# 1. rows and columns
dim(timecourse)

[1] 2323    4

# 2. the time points
unique(timecourse$Timepoint)

[1]  0  4  8 12 16 18

# 3. each combination only once
timecourse_treatments <- unique(timecourse[, c("Nutrient", "Condition", "Timepoint")])
dim(timecourse_treatments)

[1] 24  3









Garrido-Oter, Ruben, Ryohei Thomas Nakano, Nina Dombrowski, Ka-Wai Ma, Alice C. McHardy, and Paul Schulze-Lefert. 2018. “Modular Traits of the Rhizobiales Root Microbiota and Their Evolutionary Relationship with Symbiotic Rhizobia.” Cell Host & Microbe 24 (1): 155–167.e5. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chom.2018.06.006.

title: 4  Data objects
text:
4.1 Data types
Everything you store in R is an object: a single number, a table, or the result of a statistical test. Everything you do with these objects is a function call.
Objects differ in two ways:
Many functions only work on certain types and structures. A mean of text makes no sense, for example. So when something does not work, the first thing to check is what kind of object you have.
These are the data types you will use most:
Numbers come in two variants: double (any number, with or without decimals) and integer (whole numbers, written with an L, like 2L). R uses doubles unless you ask for integers, and for most work you do not need to care about the difference. Both count as numeric. R knows two more data types, complex (1+4i) and raw, but you will rarely meet them in biology.
Two functions help you find out what you have:
#create some objects
character_object <- "dataset"
number_object <- c(1,4,5)

#asking with what type we work
class(character_object)

[1] "character"

class(number_object)

[1] "numeric"
#ask how long our objects are
length(character_object)

[1] 1

length(number_object)

[1] 3

title: 4  Data objects
text:
Type
Example
What it holds




character
"hello", "low_P"
text, always written in quotes


numeric
3, 14.5
numbers


logical
TRUE, FALSE
yes/no values, for example the result of a comparison






class() tells you what kind of object you have
length() tells you how many values it holds

title: 4  Data objects
text:
4.2 Data structures
The data structures you will meet most often are:

vectors
factors
matrices
lists
data frames

You do not have to tell R in advance what an object will hold. When you assign something with <-, R picks the data type and structure for you.

4.2.1 Vectors
A vector is a row of values of the same type, for example only numbers or only text. If you mix numbers and text in one vector, R turns the numbers into text.

#lets create a random vector
a_vector <- c(2, 3, 5, 7, 1) 

#show the vector we just created
a_vector

[1] 2 3 5 7 1



#asking how long your vector is
length(a_vector)

[1] 5



4.2.1.1 Vector indexing
If we want to only retrieve part of the data stored in a vector we can create a subset using the index as shown below.

square brackets [] = allow us to retrieve certain elements of a vector, i.e. [3] retrieves the 3rd element
we can combine c() and [] if we want to retrieve several elements of a vector.


#retrieve the third element stored in a vector
a_vector[3]

[1] 5



#retrieve the 1st and 3rd element by combining ``c()`` and []
a_vector[c(1,3)]

[1] 2 5



#retrieve the 1-3rd element
a_vector[c(1:3)]

[1] 2 3 5



#we can also add vectors of the same length together
x <- c(1,2,3,4)
y <- c(1,2,3,4)

#and now we can combine our vectors
x + y

[1] 2 4 6 8


Be careful when you add two vectors of different lengths. R then repeats the shorter vector until it is as long as the longer one. This is called recycling:

#adding vectors of different lengths
x <- c(1,2)
y <- c(1,2,3,4)

#x is repeated: 1+1, 2+2, 1+3, 2+4
x + y

[1] 2 4 4 6


If the length of the longer vector is not a multiple of the shorter one, R still recycles, but gives a warning. A warning is not an error: you still get a result, so read warnings carefully.

#x is repeated, but does not fit: 1+1, 2+2, 1+3
x <- c(1,2)
y <- c(1,2,3)
x + y

Warning in x + y: longer object length is not a multiple of shorter object
length


[1] 2 4 4


Another way to extend vectors is:

append() –> Add elements to a vector.


#add another datapoint to our vector
a_vector <- append(a_vector, 13)
a_vector

[1]  2  3  5  7  1 13



#add +1 to all our four numbers
a_vector <- a_vector + 1
a_vector

[1]  3  4  6  8  2 14



#remove the first element of our vector
a_vector <- a_vector[-1]
a_vector

[1]  4  6  8  2 14


We can also give the elements of a vector names, and then use the names to get data:

#create a vector and give it names (i.e. for counts from some microbes)
x <- c(300, 410, 531)
names(x) <- c("Ecoli","Archaeoglobus","Ignicoccus")

#check how our data looks
x

        Ecoli Archaeoglobus    Ignicoccus 
          300           410           531 



#now we can retrieve part of the vector using the names
x[c("Ecoli","Ignicoccus")]

     Ecoli Ignicoccus 
       300        531 




4.2.1.2 Changing vectors
We can also change elements in our vector:

#create a vector
x <- 1:10

#change the second last positions to 5 and 9
x[9:10] <- c(5,9)

#check if this worked
x

 [1] 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 5 9



#we can not only add things, we can also remove this using the minus symbol
#i.e. lets remove the third element in our vector
x[-3]

[1] 1 2 4 5 6 7 8 5 9

#if we want to remove more than one thing we can use the **c()**
#lets remove elements 4 until (and including) 9
x[-c(4:9)]

[1] 1 2 3 9




4.2.1.3 Useful functions for vectors
Apart from the basic math operators, R has many functions that work on vectors. Some common ones are log(), exp(), sqrt() and the following:



Name
Function




max()
select the largest element


min()
select the smallest element


length()
give the number of elements


sum()
sum all elements


mean()
calculate the mean value


var()
calculate the sample variance


sort()
sort the elements from small to large




#create a vector
x <- c(4, 8, 1, 5)

#try some of the functions
max(x)

[1] 8

mean(x)

[1] 4.5

sort(x)

[1] 1 4 5 8





4.2.2 Matrices
A matrix is a table in which all values have the same type, usually numbers. You will not build many matrices yourself, but you will meet them in other people’s code and as the output of some functions, for example tables of counts or distances. Many functions that work on data frames also work on matrices, such as [rows, columns], dim() and head().

#make a matrix with the numbers 1 to 12 in 4 rows, filled row by row
matrix_A <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)

#check how our matrix looks
matrix_A

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6
[3,]    7    8    9
[4,]   10   11   12



#the value in the 2nd row and 3rd column
matrix_A[2,3]

[1] 6

#the number of rows and columns
dim(matrix_A)

[1] 4 3




4.2.3 Lists
A list is a collection of objects that can each have a different type and length: a few numbers, some text, a whole table, or even another list. You create a list with list().
For example, here we store cell counts (numeric), the names of the microbes (character) and whether they are alive (logical) in one list:

#define our vectors
n = c(20, 30, 50) 
s = c("Ecoli", "Archaeoglobus", "Bacillus") 
b = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE) 

#combine the vectors in a list
our_list = list(counts=n, strain=s, status=b) 

#show our list
our_list

$counts
[1] 20 30 50

$strain
[1] "Ecoli"         "Archaeoglobus" "Bacillus"     

$status
[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE


You get one element out of a list with $ and its name, the same way you get one column out of a data frame:

#get the element with the name strain
our_list$strain

[1] "Ecoli"         "Archaeoglobus" "Bacillus"     


Why should you care about lists? Because the results of many functions are lists. For example, a t-test (which we use in the statistics chapter) gives you a list with the test statistic, the p-value and more. With names() you see what is inside, and with $ you take out the part you need:

#compare the root length between the two phosphate levels
result <- t.test(Rootlength ~ Nutrient, data = growth_data)

#what kind of object is this, and what is inside?
class(result)

[1] "htest"

names(result)

 [1] "statistic"   "parameter"   "p.value"     "conf.int"    "estimate"   
 [6] "null.value"  "stderr"      "alternative" "method"      "data.name"  

#take out only the p-value
result$p.value

[1] 7.324612e-68




4.2.4 Dataframes
You already know data frames from the chapter “First steps in R”: our growth data is one. A data frame is a table in which each column is a vector. All columns have the same length, and each column has one data type, but different columns can have different types. In our growth data, Nutrient is text and Rootlength is numeric. So a data frame is a bit like a list of vectors of equal length.
Everything you learned about [rows, columns] and $ in “First steps in R” works on data frames. A few more functions are useful to look at them:

#the column names
colnames(growth_data)

[1] "Nutrient"    "Condition"   "Experiment"  "Rootlength"  "FW_shoot_mg"

#the first few row names
head(rownames(growth_data))

[1] "1" "2" "3" "4" "5" "6"


When you read a table into R, the rows get the numbers 1 to 594 as row names, unless you say otherwise.
You add a new column with $ and a new column name. Here we fill all rows with the word comment:

#add a new column
growth_data$newColumn <- "comment"

#check if that worked
head(growth_data)


  



You will see this way of adding columns often in other people’s code. In the next chapter you learn another way, mutate().

title: 4  Data objects
section: 4.3 Check the structure of our data
text:
4.3 Check the structure of our data
When you read in your own data, check how R stored it:

class() tells you what kind of object you have
str() (short for structure) shows the data type of each column and the first few values


#check what kind of data we have:
class(growth_data)

[1] "data.frame"



#check how are different parts of our data stored?
str(growth_data)

'data.frame':   594 obs. of  6 variables:
 $ Nutrient   : chr  "low_P" "low_P" "low_P" "low_P" ...
 $ Condition  : chr  "mock" "mock" "mock" "mock" ...
 $ Experiment : chr  "ex61" "ex61" "ex61" "ex61" ...
 $ Rootlength : num  40.4 38 74.7 34.4 31.9 66.5 34.8 43.4 33.9 41.9 ...
 $ FW_shoot_mg: num  6.6 6.8 8.1 8.3 8.6 8.9 9.5 9.8 10 10.2 ...
 $ newColumn  : chr  "comment" "comment" "comment" "comment" ...


We see that

our data is stored in a data frame
the columns have different data types: chr (character) and num (numeric)
our data contains 594 observations (rows) and 6 variables (columns): the 5 columns of our file plus the column newColumn we added above

title: 4  Data objects
text:
4.4 Factors
A factor is a vector for categorical data: data that falls into a fixed set of groups, such as our nutrient levels or treatments. The possible groups are called levels. Factors matter for statistics and for plotting, for example because the order of the levels sets the order of the groups in a plot. By default, R sorts the levels alphabetically.
You make a factor with factor():

#lets make a vector
Nutrients <- c("low_P", "low_P", "high_P", "high_P")

#lets make our own simple factor
Nutrients_factor <- factor(Nutrients)

#lets compare the vector and factor we generated
Nutrients

[1] "low_P"  "low_P"  "high_P" "high_P"

Nutrients_factor

[1] low_P  low_P  high_P high_P
Levels: high_P low_P


When we check our factor, we see that R assigns one level to low_P and another level to high_P. We can also see that R sorts the levels in alphabetical order, i.e. first we have high_P and then low_P, even though in our vector low_P came first.

4.4.1 Checking the behaviour of factors
Now, lets check how factors behave.

levels() shows the levels of a factor
nlevels() shows how many levels there are
Factors look like text, but R stores them as whole numbers (integers), one number per level. class() shows that we have a factor, typeof() shows how R stores it:


#only print the levels
levels(Nutrients_factor)

[1] "high_P" "low_P" 



#check how many levels we have
nlevels(Nutrients_factor)

[1] 2



#what class do we have
class(Nutrients_factor)

[1] "factor"

typeof(Nutrients_factor)

[1] "integer"




4.4.2 Ordering factor levels
Often the alphabetical order is not the order you want. In a plot, you may want low_P before high_P, or the control first. With the argument levels you set the order yourself:

#check our levels
levels(Nutrients_factor)

[1] "high_P" "low_P" 



#reorder levels
Nutrients_factor_reordered <- factor(Nutrients_factor, levels = c("low_P", "high_P"))

#check our levels
levels(Nutrients_factor_reordered)

[1] "low_P"  "high_P"




4.4.3 Converting factors
Sometimes you need to turn a factor back into text. You do this with as.character(). There are similar functions for other types, such as as.numeric().

#convert our factor to a character
Nutrients_characters <- as.character(Nutrients_factor)
Nutrients_characters

[1] "low_P"  "low_P"  "high_P" "high_P"

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.1 Why learn a second way?
So far, we used functions that come with R itself. This is called base R. In this chapter you learn a second way to work with tables: the tidyverse. The tidyverse is a collection of packages that share one idea. Each function does one job, and you combine these small functions step by step into a longer analysis.
Before you start, create a new Quarto document for this chapter in your project folder, for example tidyverse.qmd.
Let’s start with a question about our growth data: what is the mean root length for each condition, in the plants grown with low phosphate?
Here is one way to answer it in base R. Don’t worry if you don’t understand every detail:
# keep the low phosphate plants that have a root length
low_P <- growth_data[growth_data$Nutrient == "low_P" & !is.na(growth_data$Rootlength), ]

# calculate the mean root length for each condition
tapply(low_P$Rootlength, low_P$Condition, mean)

    129E      13C     mock 
69.91808 64.19465 47.06848
This works, but it is hard to read. The first line does three things at once: it compares the nutrient, checks for missing values and selects rows, all inside square brackets. You have to read it from the inside out.
Here is the same question answered with the tidyverse:
growth_data |>
  filter(Nutrient == "low_P") |>
  group_by(Condition) |>
  summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE))
We get the same numbers. But now the code reads from top to bottom, almost like a sentence: take the growth data, then keep the low phosphate plants, then make groups by condition, then calculate the mean root length for each group. The |> at the end of each line means “and then”. It is called the pipe.
Because each step is one line that does one job, it is easy to change the analysis. Do you want the mean per condition and per experiment? Add one column name:
growth_data |>
  filter(Nutrient == "low_P") |>
  group_by(Condition, Experiment) |>
  summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE))

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Condition'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.
You can ignore the message about “grouped output” for now. We explain it later in this chapter.
Do you want the high phosphate plants instead? Change one word in the filter() line. This is what makes the tidyverse so handy: you build an analysis from small blocks, and you can add, remove or swap blocks without rewriting everything.
So why did we learn base R first? Because you will see it everywhere: in older scripts, in other people’s code, in answers on the internet and in the help pages. The things you learned in the previous chapters, like $, [rows, columns], vectors and data types, also stay useful in the tidyverse. From now on, this book uses the tidyverse for working with tables.

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.2 The tidyverse packages
The tidyverse contains several packages, each for one kind of task:

ggplot2 for plotting
dplyr for changing tables: filtering, sorting, adding columns, summarizing
tidyr for tidying tables, for example changing their shape
readr for reading data
tibble for tibbles, a modern version of data frames (you met them in the chapter “First steps in R”)
stringr for working with text
forcats for working with factors
purrr for repeating a task many times

Figure 5.1 shows where these tasks fit in a typical data analysis. You import your data, tidy it, and then go back and forth between transforming, plotting (visualise) and statistics (model) until you understand your data. In this chapter we focus on transforming: selecting, changing and summarizing the data in a table. The plotting chapter covers ggplot2.






Figure 5.1: The steps of a typical data analysis. Source: Wickham and Grolemund, R for Data Science.



You installed the tidyverse in the chapter First steps in R. If you skipped that, type this into the Console:

install.packages("tidyverse")

Then load the tidyverse at the top of your document:

# load the tidyverse
library(tidyverse)

The tidyverse also has its own functions to read data, in the package readr. Our growth data is a tab-separated file (tsv, for tab-separated values), so we read it with read_tsv():

# read in the growth data
growth_data <- read_tsv("data/Growth_Data.txt")

Rows: 594 Columns: 5
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: "\t"
chr (3): Nutrient, Condition, Experiment
dbl (2): Rootlength, FW_shoot_mg

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


read_tsv() tells you which data type it picked for each column: chr (character) for Nutrient, Condition and Experiment, and dbl (double, a number) for the two measurements. Check this message every time you read data. If a column of numbers is read as chr, there is probably some text in it, for example a typo or a comment.
Compared with read.table(), you need fewer arguments: read_tsv() knows that the columns are separated by tabs and that the first line holds the column names. It also reads empty cells as missing values (NA).
read_tsv() gives you a tibble, like read_excel() in the chapter “First steps in R”. When you print a tibble, you only see the first 10 rows, and R tells you how many rows the table has:

growth_data


  



In this book and in your Quarto document, the tibble is shown as a table with pages. The number of rows is below the table, for example “1-10 of 594 rows”, and you can click through the pages. The data type of each column is shown under its name. In the Console, the first line tells you the number of rows and columns instead, for example # A tibble: 594 × 5.
This is very handy in this chapter. After each step, you see how many rows are left, without printing hundreds of rows.

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.3 Pipes and shortcuts
The pipe |> takes what is on its left and puts it into the function on its right, as the first argument. These two lines do the same:

head(growth_data)
growth_data |> head()

With one function, the pipe does not help much. It gets useful when you chain several functions, as in the example above. We will write each step on its own line, with the pipe at the end of the line.
You will also see a second pipe, %>%, in a lot of code. It is the older version, from before R had its own pipe. For what we do in this book, both work the same. We use |>, which needs R 4.1 or newer.
Two keyboard shortcuts make your life easier:

Ctrl+Shift+M (Cmd+Shift+M on Mac) types a pipe. By default, RStudio types %>%. To get |>, go to Tools > Global Options > Code and tick “Use native pipe operator”.
Tab completes what you are typing. Type filt and press Tab to see all functions that start with these letters.

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
section: 5.4 A first look at the data
text:
5.4 A first look at the data
You already know head() and str(). A third function, summary(), gives you a quick overview of each column:

summary(growth_data)

   Nutrient          Condition          Experiment          Rootlength    
 Length:594         Length:594         Length:594         Min.   : 28.73  
 Class :character   Class :character   Class :character   1st Qu.: 56.60  
 Mode  :character   Mode  :character   Mode  :character   Median : 75.64  
                                                          Mean   : 75.19  
                                                          3rd Qu.: 92.25  
                                                          Max.   :135.49  
                                                          NA's   :15      
  FW_shoot_mg   
 Min.   : 1.56  
 1st Qu.:12.10  
 Median :15.20  
 Mean   :16.58  
 3rd Qu.:19.63  
 Max.   :47.60  
 NA's   :8      


For the text columns, summary() only tells you how many values there are. For the numeric columns, it shows the smallest and largest value, the mean, the median and the quartiles. It also counts the missing values (NA's): 15 plants have no root length, and 8 plants have no shoot weight. We come back to these later.

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.5 Filter rows with filter()
filter() keeps the rows that meet a condition (Figure 5.2).






Figure 5.2: filter() keeps the rows that meet a condition. Source: RStudio cheatsheet Data transformation with dplyr.



For example, to keep only the plants grown with low phosphate:

growth_data |>
  filter(Nutrient == "low_P")


  



== means “is equal to”. Note that it has two equal signs: a single = is used for arguments. Text, like "low_P", always goes in quotes.
The result has 300 rows instead of 594. But growth_data itself has not changed: filter() only shows the result. If you want to keep it, store it in a new object:

# store the low phosphate plants in a new object
low_P_data <- growth_data |>
  filter(Nutrient == "low_P")

# check the number of rows
nrow(low_P_data)

[1] 300


Here is the same filter in base R, which you will see in other people’s code:

growth_data[growth_data$Nutrient == "low_P", ]

You need to write growth_data twice, plus the brackets and the comma. In filter(), you just write the column name.
These are the comparison operators you can use in filter():



Operator
Meaning




==
equal to


!=
not equal to


<
less than


<=
less than or equal to


>
greater than


>=
greater than or equal to


!
not


&
and


|
or



For example, by using != "mock" we can remove all mock plants, so we keep only the plants with bacteria:

growth_data |>
  filter(Condition != "mock")


  



And > works on numbers. We could for example only list plants that have roots longer than 100 mm:

growth_data |>
  filter(Rootlength > 100)


  




5.5.1 Filter on more than one column
You can give filter() several conditions, separated by a comma. A row is kept only if it meets all conditions:

# plants grown with low phosphate and with strain 129E
growth_data |>
  filter(Nutrient == "low_P", Condition == "129E")


  





5.5.2 Filter for several values with %in%
What if you want the plants of both strains, 129E and 13C? One way is the “or” operator |:

growth_data |>
  filter(Condition == "129E" | Condition == "13C") |>
  nrow()

[1] 385


Here we added nrow() at the end of the pipe, to count the rows instead of printing the whole table.
With many values, this means a lot of typing. %in% is shorter. It checks whether a value is in a vector:

# the conditions we want to keep
strains <- c("129E", "13C")

growth_data |>
  filter(Condition %in% strains) |>
  nrow()

[1] 385


A vector like strains is easy to read, easy to extend and you can use it again later.


5.5.3 Exercise

How many plants were grown in experiment ex64?
How many plants grown with high phosphate have a shoot weight of 20 mg or more?







TipSolution






# 1. plants in experiment ex64
growth_data |>
  filter(Experiment == "ex64") |>
  nrow()

[1] 205

# 2. high phosphate plants with a shoot weight of at least 20 mg
growth_data |>
  filter(Nutrient == "high_P", FW_shoot_mg >= 20) |>
  nrow()

[1] 137


There are 205 plants from experiment ex64, and 137 high phosphate plants with a shoot weight of at least 20 mg.

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.6 Select columns with select()
filter() chooses rows, select() chooses columns. You list the columns you want to keep:

growth_data |>
  select(Condition, Rootlength)


  



With ! you remove columns instead. To remove more than one, put them in c():

# keep all columns except Experiment and FW_shoot_mg
growth_data |>
  select(!c(Experiment, FW_shoot_mg))


  



Selection helpers select columns by a pattern in their name:

starts_with(): the name starts with some text
ends_with(): the name ends with some text
contains(): the name contains some text


# all columns whose name starts with FW
growth_data |>
  select(starts_with("FW"))


  



In our small table, this does not save much typing. But many tables in biology have hundreds of columns, for example one per sample or per gene. Then helpers like these are very useful.

5.6.1 Exercise
Select the columns Nutrient and Condition and all columns whose name contains length.






TipSolution






growth_data |>
  select(Nutrient, Condition, contains("length"))

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.7 Remove duplicates with distinct()
distinct() keeps each value, or each combination of values, only once. It is the tidyverse version of unique(), which you used in “First steps in R”:

# each combination of nutrient and condition only once
growth_data |>
  distinct(Nutrient, Condition)

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.8 Count rows with count()
count() counts the rows for each value, or each combination of values. How many plants do we have per treatment?

growth_data |>
  count(Nutrient, Condition)


  



The column n holds the number of plants. Not all groups have the same size: we have between 87 and 107 plants per group.

5.8.1 Exercise
How many plants were measured in each experiment?






TipSolution






growth_data |>
  count(Experiment)


  



The three experiments have 194, 205 and 195 plants.

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.9 Sort rows with arrange()
arrange() sorts the rows by the values in a column (Figure 5.3). By default, it starts with the smallest value:






Figure 5.3: arrange() sorts the rows by the values in a column. Source: RStudio cheatsheet Data transformation with dplyr.




growth_data |>
  arrange(Rootlength)


  



With desc() (short for descending) you start with the largest value. This is a quick way to find extreme values, for example to spot typos in your data:

growth_data |>
  arrange(desc(Rootlength))


  



The three plants with the longest roots were all grown with high phosphate and with one of the two strains.

5.9.1 Exercise
Which plant has the highest shoot weight? In which nutrient, condition and experiment was it grown?






TipSolution






growth_data |>
  arrange(desc(FW_shoot_mg))


  



The heaviest shoot weighs 47.6 mg. It is a mock plant, grown with high phosphate in experiment ex64.

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
section: 5.10 Add or change columns with mutate()
text:
5.10 Add or change columns with mutate()
mutate() adds new columns, or changes existing ones (Figure 5.4).






Figure 5.4: mutate() adds new columns or changes existing ones. Source: RStudio cheatsheet Data transformation with dplyr.



For example, we can convert the shoot weight from mg to g. Before the =, you write the name of the new column. After the =, you say how to calculate it. The new column is added at the end of the table:

# convert mg to g (1 g = 1000 mg)
growth_data |>
  mutate(FW_shoot_g = FW_shoot_mg / 1000)


  



In base R, you would write growth_data$FW_shoot_g <- growth_data$FW_shoot_mg / 1000, as in the chapter “Data objects”.
You can also calculate with several columns, and make several new columns in one mutate(), separated by commas:

growth_data |>
  mutate(FW_shoot_g = FW_shoot_mg / 1000,
         root_shoot_ratio = Rootlength / FW_shoot_mg)


  



Any calculation with a missing value gives a missing value. Rows 32 and 33 have no shoot weight, so their ratio is NA too. slice() shows rows by their number:

growth_data |>
  mutate(root_shoot_ratio = Rootlength / FW_shoot_mg) |>
  slice(32:33)


  




5.10.1 Exercise
Add a column with the root length in cm.






TipSolution






# 1 cm = 10 mm
growth_data |>
  mutate(Rootlength_cm = Rootlength / 10)

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.12 Missing values
summary() showed us that our data has missing values: 15 in Rootlength and 8 in FW_shoot_mg. Many calculations give NA if one of the values is missing. What you do about it depends on your question. Here we look at two ways to remove rows with missing values.
drop_na() removes every row that has a missing value in any column:

growth_data |>
  drop_na() |>
  nrow()

[1] 571


filter() together with is.na() removes only the rows with a missing value in one column. is.na() is TRUE for a missing value, and ! turns it around, so we keep the rows that are not missing:

growth_data |>
  filter(!is.na(Rootlength)) |>
  nrow()

[1] 579


drop_na() removes 23 rows, filter() only 15. None of our plants misses both measurements. So drop_na() also throws away 8 plants that do have a root length, only because their shoot weight is missing. If you analyse the root length, this is good data lost. Only remove the missing values you need to remove.
You can also give drop_na() the name of a column. Then it only looks at that column, and drop_na(Rootlength) does the same as our filter().

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
section: 5.13 Summarize data with group_by() and summarize()
text:
5.13 Summarize data with group_by() and summarize()
summarize() turns many rows into one row, for example by calculating a mean (Figure 5.5).






Figure 5.5: summarize() turns many rows into one. Source: RStudio cheatsheet Data transformation with dplyr.




growth_data |>
  summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE))


  



na.rm = TRUE tells mean() to ignore the missing values. Without it, the mean would be NA.
One mean for all plants is not very useful, because our plants got different treatments. This is where group_by() comes in. It splits the table into groups, and summarize() then calculates one row for each group (Figure 5.6).






Figure 5.6: group_by() before summarize() turns each group into one row. Source: RStudio cheatsheet Data transformation with dplyr.



Let’s calculate the mean and the standard deviation of the root length for each treatment, and count the plants. You can calculate several things in one summarize(), separated by commas:

growth_data |>
  group_by(Nutrient, Condition) |>
  summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_root = sd(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_plants = sum(!is.na(Rootlength))) |>
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Nutrient'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.



  



To count the plants, we use sum(!is.na(Rootlength)). !is.na() is TRUE for each plant that has a root length, and sum() counts the TRUE values. This way, we only count the plants that were used for the mean. Compare the numbers with the output of count() above: in some groups, a few plants have no root length.
Functions that are useful inside summarize():



Function
Calculates




mean(), median()
the center of the data


sd(), IQR()
the spread of the data


min(), max()
the smallest and largest value


n()
the number of rows in the group









NoteWhy ungroup()?



group_by() does not change how the table looks, but it remembers the groups. After a summarize() with two grouping columns, the result is still grouped by the first one. R tells you this with a message like “summarise() has grouped output by ‘Nutrient’”. All functions that come after it in the pipe then work per group, which can give surprising results. ungroup() removes the groups. Make it a habit to end with ungroup(), especially when you store the result in an object.



5.13.1 Exercise
Calculate the mean and the median shoot weight for each combination of nutrient and condition.






TipSolution






growth_data |>
  group_by(Nutrient, Condition) |>
  summarize(mean_shoot = mean(FW_shoot_mg, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_shoot = median(FW_shoot_mg, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Nutrient'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.



  












TipOptional: the same calculation for several columns with across()





If you want the mean of both the root length and the shoot weight, you can write two lines in summarize(). With many columns, across() saves typing. It applies the same function to several columns:

growth_data |>
  group_by(Nutrient, Condition) |>
  summarize(across(c(Rootlength, FW_shoot_mg), ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE))) |>
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Nutrient'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.



  



The ~ starts a small function, and .x stands for each column in turn. So ~ mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE) means “calculate the mean of this column, without the missing values”. The new columns keep the names of the old ones.

title: 5  Working with the tidyverse
text:
5.14 Combine tables with left_join()
In “First steps in R”, you combined two tables with merge(). The tidyverse version is left_join(). Let’s make a small table that says, for each condition, whether the plants got bacteria:

inoculation <- data.frame(Condition = c("mock", "129E", "13C"),
                          Bacteria = c("no", "yes", "yes"))

inoculation


  



Now we add this information to our growth data. The argument by says which column to use for matching the rows:

growth_with_info <- growth_data |>
  left_join(inoculation, by = "Condition")

head(growth_with_info)


  



As with merge(), always check the number of rows after a join. We still want 594 rows, one per plant:

nrow(growth_data)

[1] 594

nrow(growth_with_info)

[1] 594


Two differences to merge() with its default settings:

left_join() keeps all rows of the first table (the one on the left), also when they have no match in the second table. The new columns are then NA. merge() drops these rows, unless you add all.x = TRUE.
left_join() keeps the order of the rows of the first table. merge() sorts the rows by the by columns.







WarningMatching on too few columns



The mistake from “First steps in R” can happen here too. Let’s make a mapping file with distinct() and join on Condition only, although each condition appears twice in the mapping file (once per nutrient):

mapping_file <- growth_data |>
  distinct(Nutrient, Condition) |>
  mutate(Source = "Fig S5A,B")

wrong_join <- growth_data |>
  left_join(mapping_file, by = "Condition")

Warning in left_join(growth_data, mapping_file, by = "Condition"): Detected an unexpected many-to-many relationship between `x` and `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `x` matches multiple rows in `y`.
ℹ Row 1 of `y` matches multiple rows in `x`.
ℹ If a many-to-many relationship is expected, set `relationship =
  "many-to-many"` to silence this warning.

nrow(wrong_join)

[1] 1188


Again, each plant matches two rows and is copied. Unlike merge(), left_join() warns you about this: it reports a “many-to-many relationship”. Read warnings like this carefully. The fix is the same as before: match on both columns with by = c("Nutrient", "Condition").

title: 6  Control Structures
text:
6.1 Loops
Control structures in R allow you to control the flow of execution of a series of R expressions. Basically, control structures allow you to put some ‘logic’ into your R code, rather than just always executing the same R code every time.
Sometimes it is necessary to repeat a calculation multiple times, e.g. calculate the sum of each row of a matrix. You can use for loops to do this.
Lets assume a simple matrix with 5 rows and 3 columns. How would we generate the sum of each row?
We could do so, by calculating the sum step-by-step:
#build a dataframe
m <- matrix(1:15, 5)
m

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    6   11
[2,]    2    7   12
[3,]    3    8   13
[4,]    4    9   14
[5,]    5   10   15
#sum rows without a loop --> sum row 1
sum(m[1, ])

[1] 18
#sum rows without a loop --> sum row 2, ...
sum(m[2, ])

[1] 21
However, you will quickly see that this becomes quite tedious. So lets do this via a loop, in which we:
#run a loop to get the sum for all five rows
for (i in 1:5) {
print(sum(m[i, ]))
}

[1] 18
[1] 21
[1] 24
[1] 27
[1] 30
How would we store our results in a new dataframe and do not just print them to the screen? To do this, we:
#store the results, Note that here, the variable results had to be created before as an empty vector.
results <- c()
for (i in 1:5) {
results[i] <- sum(m[i, ])
}

results

[1] 18 21 24 27 30
Very often, there are some R packages or functions that are faster than loops.
The apply() function is such an example. apply() applies a function, i.e. sum, across a matrix.
However, since loops are also a very useful feature in bash or python it is useful to understand their general concept.
#way to do the same using the apply function (faster than loops)
results2 <- apply(m, 1, sum)
results2

[1] 18 21 24 27 30
Apply takes the following arguments:
Actually, there is a family of apply functions, depending on the object you pass as an input, and/or the object you want as output. You can read a brief tutorial under this link.
Two other examples are sapply and lapply, which work on lists.

{} –> defines the operation we want to loop through

so in i we store the numbers 1,2,3,4 and 5 and then run through the sum functions 5x
