title: 6  Control Structures
text:
6.2 if-else
One can also create a decision making structure in R. A decision making structure has at least one condition to be evaluated together with a statement or statements to be evaluated if the condition is TRUE, and optionally, other statements to be executed if the condition is FALSE, as we can see in the figure.
The test_expression has to be logical, i.e., it has to be a expression that, when evaluated, is either TRUE or FALSE. The logical operators listed above can be used to construct them. For example, we can use an if-else statement to check if a number is positive or negative,

#store a random number
x <- -5

#write a loop and ask if our number is positive or negative
if (x > 0) {
print("Positive number")
} else if (x == 0) {
print("Number is zero")
} else {
print("Negative number")
}

[1] "Negative number"


Note that in the example there was an else if. In that way we can check more than 2 conditions.
This of course is a very simplistic example. But if-else statements can be useful if we want to deal with larger dataframes, i.e. our growth data.
Specifically, we want to:

Create a new column, with the name category
If a value in our Root length column is equal to or smaller than 75 mm (about the median), we want to say this category is small.
If that is not the case, we want to say it is large


#apply ifelse
growth_data$category <- ifelse(growth_data$Rootlength <= 75, "small", "large")

#check the first rows of our data
head(growth_data)


  



So the function works like this:
ifelse(our_test, value_to_return_if_test_is_true, value_to_return_if_test_is_false)
If the root length is missing (NA), the test can’t be answered, and ifelse() returns NA as well.
We can also combine different statements with the & (AND) or | (OR) symbol. I.e. we only send things in the large category if the roots are longer than 75 mm AND the shoot weight is larger than 15 mg

#apply ifelse
growth_data$category <- ifelse(growth_data$Rootlength > 75 & growth_data$FW_shoot_mg > 15, "large", "small")

#check the first rows of our data
head(growth_data)


  



What happens with the plants where the shoot weight is missing? Let’s look at them:

#show the rows where the shoot weight is missing
growth_data[is.na(growth_data$FW_shoot_mg), ]


  



Some of them are small and some are NA. Why? For the plants with roots shorter than 75 mm, the first test is already FALSE. With AND, both tests must be TRUE, so the result is FALSE, whatever the shoot weight is. R only returns NA if the answer really depends on the missing value: when the roots are longer than 75 mm, the result depends on the shoot weight, and that is unknown.

6.2.1 if_else() inside mutate()
In the chapter “Working with the tidyverse”, you added new columns with mutate(). The tidyverse also has its own version of ifelse(): if_else(), with an underscore. Together they make the first example above. Remember to load the tidyverse with library(tidyverse) first:

growth_data |>
  mutate(category = if_else(Rootlength <= 75, "small", "large")) |>
  select(Nutrient, Condition, Rootlength, category)


  



if_else() works like ifelse(), with two extras:

It is stricter: the values for TRUE and for FALSE must have the same data type. If you mix them, for example text and a number, you get an error instead of a silent conversion.
With the argument missing, you can say what to return when the test gives NA.

Because the result is a normal column, you can use it in the next step of the pipe right away. For example, to count the plants in each category:

growth_data |>
  mutate(category = if_else(Rootlength <= 75, "small", "large", missing = "not measured")) |>
  count(Condition, category)


  



If you need more than two categories, have a look at case_when(). It works like the if, else if and else example at the start of this section.

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.1 Why plot your data?
In this chapter you learn how to plot your data. We start with a few quick plots in base R, and then spend most of the chapter on ggplot2, the plotting package of the tidyverse.
As always, load the tidyverse and read the data first. This time we need both the growth data and the timecourse data:
Plots are not only for papers and presentations. They are one of the best ways to check your data before you run any statistics. Summary numbers can hide a lot. Figure 7.1 shows a famous example: four small data sets with almost the same mean, variance and regression line, but with very different patterns. Only the first one is described well by a straight line. Without plotting, you would never notice.
So make it a habit to plot your data first, and look at it.

title: 7  Plotting your data
text: Figure 7.1: Anscombe’s quartet: four data sets with almost identical summary statistics and the same regression line (blue). Source: Wikipedia, Anscombe’s quartet.

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.2 Quick plots in base R
Base R has its own plotting functions. They are not as flexible as ggplot2, but for a quick look at your data they are often faster to type. You will also see them a lot in other people’s code, and we use some of them in the statistics chapter.
plot() draws a scatter plot. Like lm() and t.test(), it takes a formula: y ~ x, read as “y depends on x”, and the data frame with data:

# root length against shoot weight
plot(Rootlength ~ FW_shoot_mg, data = growth_data)








Plants with a missing root length or shoot weight are simply left out.
hist() draws a histogram. It takes a single column, which we get with $:

# distribution of the root length
hist(growth_data$Rootlength)








boxplot() draws a boxplot per group:

# root length per nutrient level
boxplot(Rootlength ~ Nutrient, data = growth_data)








A boxplot summarizes the values of each group:

the thick line in the box is the median: half of the values are above it, half below
the box goes from the first to the third quartile, so it holds the middle 50% of the values
the whiskers (the thin lines) go to the most extreme values that are no further than 1.5 times the height of the box away from the box
values further away are drawn as single points. They are often called outliers, but that does not mean that they are wrong

All three functions take arguments for labels, for example xlab, ylab and main (the title):

boxplot(Rootlength ~ Nutrient, data = growth_data,
        xlab = "Phosphate level", ylab = "Root length (mm)", main = "Root length")








For quick checks, this is all you need. For plots with colors, groups and several panels, base R code quickly gets long and hard to read. This is where ggplot2 is much easier.

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.3 Your first ggplot
Every ggplot is built from the same parts:

ggplot() starts the plot. You give it the data frame, and in aes() (short for aesthetics) you say which column goes on which axis.
A geom says how to draw the data, for example as points (geom_point()), boxes (geom_boxplot()) or lines (geom_line()).
The parts are added to each other with +. Each part is a layer of the plot.

Let’s make the same scatter plot as above:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 23 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Notice the warning that starts with “Removed 23 rows containing missing values”. ggplot2 leaves out the plants with a missing root length (15) or a missing shoot weight (8), just like base R. But unlike base R, it tells you about it. This is not an error: the plot is still made. Now that we know what the warning means, we hide it in the rest of this chapter with #| warning: false at the top of the chunks.
Always put the + at the end of a line, not at the start of the next one. Otherwise R thinks the plot is finished after the first line.

7.3.1 Exercise
Plot the root length (y-axis) against the condition (x-axis). What is different from the plot above?






TipSolution






ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength)) +
  geom_point()








Because Condition is text and not a number, ggplot2 makes one column of points per condition. Many points lie on top of each other, so it is hard to see how many plants there are. We fix this later with boxplots and geom_jitter().

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.4 Store and save your plots
You can store a plot in an object, like any other result in R. To see the plot, type the name of the object:

root_shoot_plot <- ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength)) +
  geom_point()

root_shoot_plot








ggsave() saves a plot to a file. The file type comes from the file name, for example .pdf, .png or .svg. With width, height and units you set the size:

ggsave("output_examples/Plot_root_length.pdf", plot = root_shoot_plot,
       width = 12, height = 10, units = "cm")

For figures in a paper or a poster, save your plots as vector files, such as pdf or svg. A vector file stores lines and points as shapes, so you can zoom in without losing quality, and you can still change details in programs like Inkscape or Illustrator. Raster files, such as png or jpg, store pixels. They are fine for slides and websites.
You can also save the plot that you see in the Plots pane with the Export button above the plot.

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.5 Aesthetics: colors, shapes and more
So far, we put columns on the x- and y-axis. In aes(), you can also link columns to other properties of the plot, for example:

color: the color of points and lines
fill: the color inside boxes and bars
shape: the shape of points
linetype: solid, dashed or dotted lines

Let’s color the points by nutrient level:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength, color = Nutrient)) +
  geom_point()








ggplot2 picks the colors and adds a legend for us.
There is an important difference between setting a property inside and outside aes():

Inside aes(), you link the property to a column: each nutrient level gets its own color.
Outside aes(), in the geom, you give a fixed value for all points.

For example, to make all points blue and a bit transparent (with alpha, from 0 for invisible to 1 for solid):

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", alpha = 0.4)









7.5.1 Exercise
Make the scatter plot again. Color the points by condition, and give each nutrient level its own shape.






TipSolution






ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength, color = Condition, shape = Nutrient)) +
  geom_point()

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.6 Geoms: different types of plots
To change the type of plot, you change the geom. Here are the ones you will use most.

7.6.1 Boxplots

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength)) +
  geom_boxplot()








A boxplot hides how many plants there are. You can show them by adding the points as a second layer. geom_jitter() draws the points with a bit of random sideways noise, so they don’t lie on top of each other. With width you set how far they spread:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3)








outlier.shape = NA hides the outlier points of the boxplot. Otherwise these plants would be drawn twice: once by the boxplot and once by geom_jitter().
With fill, we get one box per nutrient level within each condition:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength, fill = Nutrient)) +
  geom_boxplot()










7.6.2 Histograms
A histogram only needs the x-axis. ggplot2 counts how many plants fall into each interval (bin). With binwidth you set the width of the bins, here 5 mm:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Rootlength)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)








To compare the nutrient levels, we fill the bars by nutrient. position = "identity" draws the two histograms on top of each other instead of stacking them, and alpha makes them transparent, so we can see both:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Rootlength, fill = Nutrient)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, position = "identity", alpha = 0.5)










7.6.3 Line plots
Line plots are good for measurements over time, like our timecourse data. We don’t want a line through every single plant, but through the mean of each group at each time point. So we first summarize the data with group_by() and summarize(), as in the chapter “Working with the tidyverse”:

# mean root length per nutrient, condition and time point
timecourse_summary <- timecourse |>
  group_by(Nutrient, Condition, Timepoint) |>
  summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength)) |>
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Nutrient', 'Condition'. You can override
using the `.groups` argument.

timecourse_summary


  



Let’s plot the plants grown with low phosphate. color = Condition gives us one line per condition, and we add the points on top of the lines:

timecourse_summary |>
  filter(Nutrient == "low_P") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Timepoint, y = mean_root, color = Condition)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()








Notice that we can give the result of a pipe straight to ggplot(). After ggplot(), the layers are joined with +, not with |>.


7.6.4 Trend lines
geom_smooth() adds a trend line to a scatter plot. With method = "lm" it draws the straight line of a linear model, which you will learn about in the statistics chapter. The grey band shows how uncertain the line is:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")








If you color by a column, you get one line per group:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength, color = Nutrient)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")










7.6.5 Exercise

Make a boxplot of the shoot weight per condition, with the plants shown as points.
Make a line plot of the timecourse for the plants grown with high phosphate.







TipSolution






# 1. shoot weight per condition
ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = FW_shoot_mg)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3)







# 2. timecourse with high phosphate
timecourse_summary |>
  filter(Nutrient == "high_P") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Timepoint, y = mean_root, color = Condition)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.7 Bar graphs with error bars
In biology, you often see bar graphs that show the mean of each group with error bars. For this, we first make a table with the mean and the standard deviation of each group. The standard deviation (sd) describes how much the root length varies between the plants of a group: the larger it is, the more the plants differ from each other.

# mean and standard deviation of the root length per treatment
root_summary <- growth_data |>
  group_by(Nutrient, Condition) |>
  summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_root = sd(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Nutrient'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.

root_summary


  



geom_col() draws bars with the height that is given in the data. geom_errorbar() draws the error bars, from ymin to ymax:

ggplot(root_summary, aes(x = Condition, y = mean_root, fill = Nutrient)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge()) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_root - sd_root, ymax = mean_root + sd_root),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.2)








position_dodge() puts the bars of the two nutrient levels next to each other instead of on top of each other. The error bars need the same dodge, so that they end up on top of the right bar.






ImportantWhat do the error bars show?



Error bars can show different things: the standard deviation, the standard error of the mean, or a confidence interval. These can differ a lot in size for the same data, so a reader can only interpret your error bars if you say which one you use. Always write it in the figure legend, for example “mean ± sd”. The statistics chapter shows how large the difference between sd and se can be.


A bar graph only shows the mean of each group and hides everything else. A boxplot with the points, as above, shows how the plants are spread and how many there are. Think about which plot tells your reader more.

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.8 Order of the groups
ggplot2 sorts text columns alphabetically. That is why 129E and 13C come before mock, and high_P before low_P. Often you want another order, for example with the control first.
Remember factors from the chapter “Data objects”? The order of the levels sets the order in the plot. With mutate() and factor(), we set the order ourselves:

growth_data <- growth_data |>
  mutate(Condition = factor(Condition, levels = c("mock", "129E", "13C")),
         Nutrient = factor(Nutrient, levels = c("low_P", "high_P")))

Now the control comes first, and low phosphate before high phosphate:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength, fill = Nutrient)) +
  geom_boxplot()

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.9 Facets: one panel per group
Sometimes a plot gets clearer if you split it into several panels, one per group. This is called faceting. facet_wrap() makes one panel for each value of a column. The ~ reads as “by”:

ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ Nutrient)








By default, all panels have the same axes, which makes it easy to compare them. With scales = "free_y", each panel gets its own y-axis. And with ncol or nrow you set how the panels are arranged.

7.9.1 Exercise
Plot the timecourse for both nutrient levels, with one panel per nutrient level.






TipSolution






ggplot(timecourse_summary, aes(x = Timepoint, y = mean_root, color = Condition)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ Nutrient)

title: 7  Plotting your data
text:
7.10 Labels, colors and themes
The default plots are good for a first look. For a report or a paper, you usually want better labels, your own colors and a cleaner look.

labs() sets the axis titles, the legend title and a plot title.
scale_fill_manual() sets your own colors for fill (and scale_color_manual() for color). You can name the colors, so that each group gets the right one.
A theme sets the overall look. theme_classic() has no grey background and no grid lines. Other built-in themes are, for example, theme_bw() and theme_minimal().
theme() changes single parts of the plot, for example where the legend goes.


root_plot <- ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength, fill = Nutrient)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(low_P = "grey80", high_P = "grey30")) +
  labs(x = "Condition", y = "Root length (mm)", fill = "Phosphate") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

root_plot








Colors can be given by name, like "grey80", or as a hex code, like "#2A6FDB". Choose colors that people with color blindness can tell apart, and that still work when printed in grey.

For a figure with several panels, you can combine plots with ggarrange() from the ggpubr package. Install it once with install.packages("ggpubr") in the Console. We also use ggpubr in the statistics chapter.
Let’s make a second plot for the shoot weight, with the same look:

shoot_plot <- ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = FW_shoot_mg, fill = Nutrient)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(low_P = "grey80", high_P = "grey30")) +
  labs(x = "Condition", y = "Shoot fresh weight (mg)", fill = "Phosphate") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

library(ggpubr)

combined_plot <- ggarrange(root_plot, shoot_plot,
                           labels = c("A", "B"),
                           ncol = 2, nrow = 1,
                           common.legend = TRUE, legend = "bottom")

combined_plot

ggsave("output_examples/Two_plots.pdf", plot = combined_plot,
       width = 18, height = 10, units = "cm")

title: 8  Statistics in R
text:
8.2 Summary statistics per group
A mean over all plants is not very informative, because our plants got different treatments. In the chapter “Working with the tidyverse” you learned how to count rows and summarize data per group. Let’s use this to get an overview of our experiment.
First, how many plants do we have per treatment?

#count the plants for each combination of nutrient and condition
growth_data |>
  count(Nutrient, Condition)


  



The groups have slightly different sizes. For this tutorial we can ignore this as the imbalance is small, but very different group sizes can matter for some statistical tests. Counting is also a quick way to spot samples with fewer measurements than you expected.
Now we calculate the mean, the standard deviation (sd) and the standard error (se) of the root length for each treatment:

#summary statistics of the root length per treatment
growth_summary <- growth_data |>
  group_by(Nutrient, Condition) |>
  summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_root = sd(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_plants = sum(!is.na(Rootlength)),
            se_root = sd_root / sqrt(n_plants)) |>
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Nutrient'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.

growth_summary


  



The standard deviation describes how much the root length varies between the plants of a group. The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of plants. It describes how precisely we know the mean of the group: the more plants we measure, the smaller it gets. Error bars in figures often show one of the two, so always say which one you use.
To see how different the two can be, let’s plot the same bar graph as in the plotting chapter twice: once with the sd and once with the se as error bars. We first make the bars without error bars and store them, and then add the two kinds of error bars. coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 120)) gives both plots the same y-axis, so that we can compare them:

library(ggpubr)

# the bars without error bars, with the same y-axis for both plots
bars <- ggplot(growth_summary, aes(x = Condition, y = mean_root, fill = Nutrient)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge()) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 120)) +
  labs(y = "Root length (mm)")

# error bars with the standard deviation
sd_plot <- bars +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_root - sd_root, ymax = mean_root + sd_root),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "mean ± sd")

# error bars with the standard error
se_plot <- bars +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_root - se_root, ymax = mean_root + se_root),
                position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "mean ± se")

ggarrange(sd_plot, se_plot, ncol = 2, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "bottom")








It is exactly the same data, but the se bars are about ten times shorter than the sd bars. The reason is the number of plants: with 85 to 105 plants per group, the standard deviation is divided by about 10 (the square root of 100). The plants within a group still vary a lot in root length (the sd is between 11 and 17 mm), but we know the mean of each group quite precisely (the se is below 2 mm).
So what small error bars tell you depends on what they show. Small sd bars mean that the plants within a group are similar. Small se bars only mean that the mean is known precisely, and that can come from similar plants, from many plants, or from both. This is why a figure legend must always say which one is shown.
Which one should you use? It depends on what your reader should see. If you want to show how variable your plants are, use the sd. If you want to compare groups, for example a treatment with the control, the se or a 95% confidence interval is usually more appropriate, because they show how precisely you know each mean (Cumming, Fidler, and Vaux 2007). Don’t choose the se only because the bars look smaller. And don’t read se bars that do not overlap as a significant difference: that is a common mistake (Krzywinski and Altman 2013). Whatever you use, write it in the figure legend together with the number of plants per group, and with small groups, show the individual data points instead.
Note that inside summarize(), you can use the columns you made earlier in the same summarize(): se_root uses sd_root and n_plants.
Other useful functions inside summarize():

mean(): the sum of all values divided by their number
median(): 50% of the values are above and 50% below this value
sd(): the standard deviation
IQR(): the interquartile range, the range of the middle 50% of the values. It is less sensitive to outliers than the standard deviation
min(), max(): the smallest and largest value
quantile(x, 0.25): 25% of the values are below this value
n(): the number of rows in the group
sum(!is.na(x)): the number of values that are not missing
n_distinct(x): the number of different values
sum(x > 10): the number of values larger than 10
mean(x > 10): the proportion of values larger than 10

In other people’s code, you will also see other ways to do the same, for example the base R functions table() to count and tapply() to calculate a mean per group, or ddply() from the older package plyr.

text:
8.3 Linear models

8.3.1 Basics
It is very simple to investigate linear relationships among variables in R. We want to estimate how a quantitative dependent variable changes according to the levels of one or more categorical independent variables. In the command below, the linear relationship between Rootlength (the dependent variable, i.e. the one we’re trying to predict) and FW_shoot_mg (the independent variable or the predictor) is calculated.
We need to use the function summary to see the results of that command; coef extracts the best-fit coefficients, anova performs an analysis of variance; there are many other extractor functions.

#is there a correlation between freshweight and root length?
linearmodel <- lm(Rootlength ~ FW_shoot_mg, data = growth_data)
linearmodel


Call:
lm(formula = Rootlength ~ FW_shoot_mg, data = growth_data)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)  FW_shoot_mg  
     45.471        1.782  



#let's extract the entire t-table
summary(linearmodel) 


Call:
lm(formula = Rootlength ~ FW_shoot_mg, data = growth_data)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-59.467 -16.619   1.126  13.202  50.139 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  45.4713     2.2970   19.80   <2e-16 ***
FW_shoot_mg   1.7818     0.1279   13.94   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 20.64 on 569 degrees of freedom
  (23 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.2544,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2531 
F-statistic: 194.2 on 1 and 569 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Here one of the values is the model p-Value (bottom last line) and the p-Value of individual predictor variables (extreme right column under ‘Coefficients’). The p-Values are very important because, we can consider a linear model to be statistically significant only when both these p-Values are less that the pre-determined statistical significance level, which is ideally 0.05. This is visually interpreted by the significance stars at the end of the row. The more the stars beside the variable’s p-Value, the more significant the variable.

Residuals: The section summarizes the residuals, the error between the prediction of the model and the actual results. Smaller residuals are better.
Coefficients: For each variable and the intercept, a weight is produced and that weight has other attributes like the standard error, a t-test value and significance.
Estimate: This is the weight given to the variable. In the simple regression case (one variable plus the intercept), it tells you by how much the root length changes, according to the model, for every increase of the shoot fresh weight by 1 mg. In our data, the estimate is 1.78: for every additional mg of shoot fresh weight, the model predicts a root that is 1.78 mm longer.

lm() automatically leaves out all plants with a missing root length or a missing shoot weight. You can see how many it removed in the line “observations deleted due to missingness” of the summary. * Std. Error: Tells you how precisely was the estimate measured. It’s really only useful for calculating the t-value. * t-value and Pr(>[t]): The t-value is calculated by taking the coefficient divided by the Std. Error. It is then used to test whether or not the coefficient is significantly different from zero. If it isn’t significant, then the coefficient really isn’t adding anything to the model and could be dropped or investigated further. Pr(>|t|) is the significance level.
Performance Measures:
Three sets of measurements are provided.

Residual Standard Error: This is the standard deviation of the residuals. Smaller is better.
Multiple / Adjusted R-Square: For one variable, the distinction doesn’t really matter. R-squared shows the amount of variance explained by the model. Adjusted R-Square takes into account the number of variables and is most useful for multiple-regression.
F-Statistic: The F-test checks if at least one variable’s weight is significantly different than zero. This is a global test to help asses a model. If the p-value is not significant (e.g. greater than 0.05) than your model is essentially not doing anything.

We also can just print parts of the data:

#print only the coefficients 
coef(summary(linearmodel))

             Estimate Std. Error  t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 45.471292  2.2969633 19.79626 9.470283e-67
FW_shoot_mg  1.781836  0.1278697 13.93478 3.480146e-38



#print only the anova stats
anova(linearmodel)


  




#plot the data and add the line of the model
plot(Rootlength ~ FW_shoot_mg, data = growth_data)
abline(linearmodel, col = "red")








If we look at the stats and the p value we see a decent correlation. However, since we tested different nutrient conditions it also can be useful to separate data to get a clearer picture. Something else to consider is to ask whether the data is normally distributed and based on that what statistical test to choose.

#color the points by nutrient condition to check this
plot(Rootlength ~ FW_shoot_mg, data = growth_data, col = factor(Nutrient))
legend("topleft", legend = c("high_P", "low_P"), col = 1:2, pch = 1)








col = factor(Nutrient) gives each nutrient level its own color: the first level gets color 1 (black), the second color 2 (red). Remember from the chapter “Data objects” that the levels are sorted alphabetically, so high_P is black and low_P is red. The legend has to list them in the same order.


8.3.2 Analysing residuals
Anyone can fit a linear model in R. The real test is to look at the residuals: the differences between the measured root lengths and the root lengths that the model predicts. The predicted values are called the fitted values. If the model describes the data well, the residuals:

are spread evenly around 0, without a pattern
have about the same spread for all fitted values (the variance is constant)
follow a normal distribution
are independent of each other, i.e. one plant does not influence another. You can’t see this in a plot; it depends on how the experiment was set up.

When you use plot() on a model, R draws diagnostic plots that help you check this. The number says which plot you want. We use the same plots later for the ANOVA.
Residuals versus fitted values

plot(linearmodel, 1)








Each point is one plant. The x-axis shows the root length that the model predicts, the y-axis the residual. The dotted line marks 0, and the red line follows the average residual from left to right. Look for two things:

If the red line clearly bends, for example like a U, the relationship between shoot weight and root length is not a straight line.
If the points spread out like a funnel, wider on one side than on the other, the variance is not constant.

R labels the three most extreme points with their row number. In our plot, the points are scattered around 0 without a clear curve, and the red line stays close to 0. It only bends down on the right, where there are few plants. Plant 176 has the largest negative residual: it is the plant with the heaviest shoot (47.6 mg) that you found in the chapter “Working with the tidyverse”. The model predicts a root length of about 130 mm for it, but its root is only 70.8 mm long.
Histogram of the residuals
resid() takes the residuals out of the model, so we can draw a histogram of them:

hist(resid(linearmodel), main = "Histogram of the residuals", xlab = "Residuals")








If the residuals follow a normal distribution, the histogram looks roughly like a bell curve around 0. Ours does.
Q-Q plot of the residuals

plot(linearmodel, 2)








If the residuals follow a normal distribution, the points lie on the dotted line. In our plot, the middle part follows the line well. At both ends, the points bend away from the line towards 0: the largest residuals are smaller than we would expect from a normal distribution. So our data has fewer extreme values than a normal distribution would have. Small deviations at the ends are common in real data, and with almost 600 plants they are not a big problem for a linear model. < Also remember the colored plot above: our data contains two nutrient levels with clearly different root lengths. A model that includes the nutrient level might describe the data better and we will look more into how to do that below.

text:
8.4 A new dataset for statistical tests
For the statistical tests in the rest of this chapter, we use a smaller and cleaner dataset from the same study (Garrido-Oter et al. 2018). Plants of three Arabidopsis genotypes were grown with or without the strain 129E, and the authors counted the number of cells in the meristem of the root tip, the zone where new root cells are made. The genotypes are:

Col-0: the wild type, i.e. the standard Arabidopsis line most labs use
ahk3-3 and arr1_arr12: two mutant lines


We use this dataset because the groups are small, similar in size and well-behaved, which makes it easier to see how the tests work. A second file with the root length of the same genotypes is used in the exercise at the end of this chapter.
Download the two files in the same way as in the first steps chapter:

# download the meristem data, but only if we don't have it yet
if (!file.exists("data/Genotype_Meristem.txt")) {
  download.file(url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/R_cookbook/main/data/Genotype_Meristem.txt",
                destfile = "data/Genotype_Meristem.txt",
                mode = "wb")
}

# download the root length data of the same genotypes, but only if we don't have it yet
if (!file.exists("data/Genotype_Rootlength.txt")) {
  download.file(url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/R_cookbook/main/data/Genotype_Rootlength.txt",
                destfile = "data/Genotype_Rootlength.txt",
                mode = "wb")
}


# read in the meristem data
meristem <- read_tsv("data/Genotype_Meristem.txt")

title: 8  Statistics in R
text:
8.5 Comparing two groups: the t-test
Let’s start with the simplest question: does 129E change the number of meristem cells in the wild type? For this, we only need the Col-0 plants:

# keep only the wild type
col0 <- meristem |>
  filter(Genotype == "Col-0")

# look at the data
boxplot(Meristem_cells ~ Condition, data = col0, ylab = "Number of meristem cells")








A t-test compares the means of two groups. It asks: if there was really no difference between the groups, how likely is a difference between the means as large as the one we see? This likelihood is the p-value. If it is smaller than 0.05, we usually call the difference statistically significant.
The t-test assumes that the values in each group come from a normal distribution. We will look at this in more detail below, but for now we check it with the Shapiro-Wilk test, once per group:

# test for normality in each group
col0 |>
  group_by(Condition) |>
  summarize(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(Meristem_cells)$p.value) |>
  ungroup()


  



shapiro.test() gives a list with several results, like t.test() in the chapter “Data objects”. With $p.value we take out only the p-value, and group_by() makes sure that we get one test per condition.
The Shapiro-Wilk test works the other way round: here, a p-value above 0.05 is what we want, because it means that there is no evidence against a normal distribution.
Now the t-test itself. The ~ reads as “depends on”: we test whether the number of meristem cells depends on the condition.

# compare mock and 129E in the wild type
t.test(Meristem_cells ~ Condition, data = col0)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  Meristem_cells by Condition
t = 3.4714, df = 19.311, p-value = 0.002508
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 129E and group mock is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
  2.988992 12.041311
sample estimates:
mean in group 129E mean in group mock 
          38.18182           30.66667 


The most important lines of the output are:

t and p-value: the test statistic and the p-value.
95 percent confidence interval: the range in which the true difference between the two means probably lies.
mean in group ...: the mean of each group.

By default, R runs the Welch version of the t-test, which does not assume that both groups have the same variance. That is why the title says “Welch Two Sample t-test”.
In our data, wild-type plants treated with 129E have on average 38.2 meristem cells, and mock plants 30.7. The difference is significant (p = 0.0025), and the confidence interval tells us that 129E adds roughly 3 to 12 cells. Both Shapiro-Wilk tests above gave p-values well above 0.05 (0.82 and 0.37), so we can use a t-test here.
If your data is clearly not normally distributed, you can use the Wilcoxon rank sum test (also called Mann-Whitney U test) instead. It does not compare the means, but uses the ranks of the values, so it does not need a normal distribution:

# a test that does not assume a normal distribution
wilcox.test(Meristem_cells ~ Condition, data = col0)

Warning in wilcox.test.default(x = DATA[[1L]], y = DATA[[2L]], ...): cannot
compute exact p-value with ties



    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  Meristem_cells by Condition
W = 114, p-value = 0.003382
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0


You may see a warning that R “cannot compute exact p-value with ties”. Ties are values that occur more than once, which is common for counts such as our cell numbers. R then calculates an approximate p-value instead, which is fine here. The Wilcoxon test comes to the same conclusion as the t-test (p = 0.003).

title: 8  Statistics in R
text:
8.6 Checking for a normal distribution
Many statistical tests, such as the t-test and the ANOVA below, assume that the values in each group come from a normal distribution. It is important to check this per group: if you put all plants together, you mix groups with different means, and the combined data will not look normal even if every group is.

8.6.1 Density plots
A density plot is a smoothed version of a histogram. In ggplot2, geom_density() draws one curve per condition, and facet_wrap() makes one panel per genotype, as in the plotting chapter. geom_rug() adds a small tick at the bottom for each plant, so you can see where the actual values are:

ggplot(meristem, aes(x = Meristem_cells, color = Condition)) +
  geom_density() +
  geom_rug() +
  facet_wrap(~ Genotype) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("129E" = "#2A6FDB", mock = "#8C8C8C")) +
  labs(x = "Number of meristem cells")








In all three genotypes, the curve of the 129E plants lies to the right of the mock curve, so treated plants tend to have more meristem cells. The shift is largest in arr1_arr12. Some curves have small bumps, for example Col-0 with 129E, but with only 11 to 15 plants per group, a density curve is never perfectly smooth.


8.6.2 Q-Q plots
A Q-Q plot (quantile-quantile plot) compares the values in a group with the values you would expect from a normal distribution. If the data is normally distributed, the points lie close to the diagonal line.
ggplot2 can draw Q-Q plots too, but here we use ggqqplot() from the ggpubr package, which we loaded above. ggpubr builds on ggplot2 and makes some common plots quicker to draw. Its Q-Q plot also adds a shaded band in the color of each group, which shows the range in which we would expect the points if the data was normally distributed. Note that ggpubr functions take the column names in quotes, and use facet.by instead of facet_wrap():

ggqqplot(meristem, x = "Meristem_cells",
         color = "Condition", palette = c("#2A6FDB", "#8C8C8C"),
         facet.by = "Genotype")








In all six groups, the points lie close to the line and inside the shaded band, so there is no sign of a strong deviation from a normal distribution.


8.6.3 Shapiro-Wilk test for each group
We already ran the Shapiro-Wilk test for the two wild-type groups. With group_by(), we can run it for all six combinations of genotype and condition at once:

# one Shapiro-Wilk test per genotype and condition
meristem |>
  group_by(Genotype, Condition) |>
  summarize(shapiro_p = shapiro.test(Meristem_cells)$p.value) |>
  ungroup()

`summarise()` has grouped output by 'Genotype'. You can override using the
`.groups` argument.



  



The Shapiro-Wilk test checks the null hypothesis that the values come from a normal distribution. If the p-value is smaller than 0.05, we reject this hypothesis and should not assume a normal distribution.
In our data, all six p-values are between 0.37 and 0.87. None of the groups deviates significantly from a normal distribution, which fits what we saw in the plots.
Keep in mind that the result of the test depends on the number of values. With small groups like ours (11 to 15 plants), the test can easily miss a deviation from the normal distribution. With very large groups, it flags even tiny deviations that don’t matter in practice. So always look at the plots as well, not only at the p-value.

title: 8  Statistics in R
text:
8.7 ANOVA
With a t-test we can compare two groups. Our data has six groups: three genotypes, each with and without 129E. To compare more than two groups, we use an analysis of variance (ANOVA).
Let’s first look at the data:

ggplot(meristem, aes(x = Genotype, y = Meristem_cells, color = Condition)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("129E" = "#2A6FDB", mock = "#8C8C8C")) +
  labs(y = "Number of meristem cells")








In every genotype, plants treated with 129E have more meristem cells than mock plants. The arr1_arr12 plants with 129E stand out, with clearly more cells than all other groups.
We start with an ANOVA that tests whether the number of meristem cells depends on the genotype and on the condition:

# two-way ANOVA, additive model
aov_add <- aov(Meristem_cells ~ Genotype + Condition, data = meristem)
summary(aov_add)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
Genotype     2   2958  1479.1   38.21 3.28e-12 ***
Condition    1   2646  2646.0   68.36 3.38e-12 ***
Residuals   76   2942    38.7                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The output has one row per factor. Pr(>F) is the p-value, and the stars at the end of the row show how small it is (see the Signif. codes line).
Both the genotype and the condition have a significant effect on the number of meristem cells (both p < 0.001).
The model above is called an additive model. It assumes that the effect of 129E is the same in every genotype. But maybe 129E has a larger effect in one genotype than in another. This is called an interaction between the two factors. To include it, we replace the + by a *:

# Two-way ANOVA with interaction effect

# These two calls are equivalent
aov_int <- aov(Meristem_cells ~ Genotype * Condition, data = meristem)
aov_int <- aov(Meristem_cells ~ Genotype + Condition + Genotype:Condition, data = meristem)

# summarize the ANOVA
summary(aov_int)

                   Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
Genotype            2 2958.1  1479.1   49.83 1.96e-14 ***
Condition           1 2646.0  2646.0   89.14 2.45e-14 ***
Genotype:Condition  2  745.3   372.7   12.55 2.02e-05 ***
Residuals          74 2196.6    29.7                     
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The new row Genotype:Condition tests the interaction. It is significant (p = 2e-05): the effect of 129E on the number of meristem cells depends on the genotype.
If the interaction is not significant, use the additive model. If it is significant, as here, keep the interaction in the model, and be careful with statements about the main effects alone: “129E increases the number of meristem cells” is then only part of the story, because the size of the effect depends on the genotype.
An interaction plot shows this well. Each line is one condition, and the points are the group means. If there is no interaction, the lines are roughly parallel:

interaction.plot(x.factor = meristem$Genotype, trace.factor = meristem$Condition,
                 response = meristem$Meristem_cells,
                 xlab = "Genotype", ylab = "Mean number of meristem cells", trace.label = "Condition")








Here the lines are clearly not parallel. In arr1_arr12, 129E adds about 20 cells on average, in ahk3-3 and Col-0 only about 7.

title: 8  Statistics in R
text:
8.8 Which groups differ? Tukey’s test
A significant ANOVA tells us that some group means differ, but not which ones. To find out, we compare all pairs of groups. Because we make many comparisons at the same time, the chance that at least one of them is significant just by chance becomes large. Tukey’s HSD (Honest Significant Differences) test corrects for this. It is a post-hoc test, which means that it is used after an ANOVA.

# compare all pairs of groups
TukeyHSD(aov_int)

The output has one block per factor. The last block, $Genotype:Condition, compares all six groups with each other. For each pair, diff is the difference between the means, lwr and upr give the 95% confidence interval of this difference, and p adj is the p-value, adjusted for the number of comparisons.
The comparisons we are most interested in are mock against 129E within the same genotype. All three are significant: ahk3-3 (p adj = 0.018), arr1_arr12 (p adj < 0.001) and Col-0 (p adj = 0.018). library(agricolae)

section: 8.9 Checking the assumptions of the ANOVA
text:
8.9 Checking the assumptions of the ANOVA
Besides a normal distribution, the ANOVA assumes that all groups have a similar variance (homogeneity of variances). We can check both assumptions on the residuals of the model, i.e. the differences between each value and the mean of its group.

8.9.1 Homogeneity of variances
The residuals versus fitted values plot shows the residuals of each group (the fitted values are the group means). The spread of the points should be similar in all groups:

plot(aov_int, 1)








R labels the three most extreme values with their row numbers. In our data, the spread is similar in all six groups, and the red line stays close to 0. Plants 39, 48 and 51 are marked as the most extreme values, but they are not far away from the rest.
We can also test this with Levene’s test from the car package. Its null hypothesis is that all groups have the same variance, so here again a p-value above 0.05 is what we want:

library(car)
leveneTest(Meristem_cells ~ Genotype * Condition, data = meristem)


  



With p = 0.30 there is no evidence that the variances differ between the groups.


8.9.2 Normality of the residuals
The Q-Q plot of the residuals should roughly follow the straight line:

plot(aov_int, 2)








The points follow the line closely, with a small deviation at the upper end (plants 39 and 48). Together with Levene’s test, this means that the assumptions of the ANOVA are met for this dataset.

9.1 The example data
This chapter uses a second, larger dataset. It is the output of the Spang_team annotation pipeline, but the workflow shown here can be used for any type of categorical data you want to summarize.
With this pipeline, we generated the file UAP2_Annotation_table_u.txt, which includes annotations for a set of 46 DPANN genomes. It lists each individual protein found across these 46 genomes, together with its annotations from several databases (arCOG, KO, PFAM, …).
Specifically, we want to learn how to:
For this to work, we have some additional files to make our job easier:
When working with genomes, we often have large lists of proteins and their annotations, often from different databases.

We might also want to plot the data to compare the presence absence levels of different genomes. This section with discuss how to do this in a step by step manner.

9.3 Deal with the mapping file for our genomes

9.3.1 Load mapping file
mapping file = a table that has the metadata for our genomes. In this specific example it lists our 46 DPANN genomes into clusters based on their phylogenetic placement.
We later want to summarize our data by individual bins and the phylogenetic clusters defined in the mapping file.

9.4 Clean mapping file
Here, we want to add an extra column that summarizes how many genomes are in each phylogenetic cluster.
First lets summarize how many bins we have for each cluster:

ddply() = summarize our data by counting the number of bins we have in each cluster
order() = next, we order our data based on the clusters with the greater number of bins


#add a new column that links the BinID and the taxonomic cluster
design$NewName2 <-paste(design$BinID, design$Cluster, sep = "-")
head(design)


  




#transform mapping file and summarize how many genomes we have/cluster
Number_of_taxa <- ddply(design, .(Cluster), summarize, NrGenomes = length(Cluster))

#order our data
Number_of_taxa <- Number_of_taxa[order(Number_of_taxa$NrGenomes, decreasing = TRUE),] 

#view data
head(Number_of_taxa)


  



Next, add this information into our original mapping file:

paste() = paste together different columns. With sep we can control what delimiter we want to use when combining info


#add a new column with the cluster count info into mapping file (then it can be added as a label into figures)
design_2 <- merge(design, Number_of_taxa, by = "Cluster" )

#view wether all went fine
head(design_2)


  



Next, let’s merge all relevant into one column using paste() again:

#generate a new column into the mapping file that links the cluster name with the number of genomes of clusters in each cluster
design_2$ClusterName <- paste(design_2$Cluster, " (", design_2$NrGenomes, ")", sep = "")

#view data
head(design_2)

9.6 Deal with mapping files for the annotations
The mapping files (Arcog_mapping and Metabolism_file_KEGG) that are provided with this tutorial give extra information and order our KO and arCOG annotations. Genes_of_interest is a list of key metabolic genes we want to look at more closely.

9.6.1 Load and view the tables

#general mapping file for arcog IDs
Arcog_mapping <- read.table("data/ar14_arCOGdef19.txt", sep="\t", header=T, fill=TRUE, quote = "")
head(Arcog_mapping)


  


#pathway mapping file
Metabolism_file_KEGG <- read.table("data/Metabolism_Table_KO_Apr2020.txt", sep="\t", header=T, fill=TRUE, quote = "")
head(Metabolism_file_KEGG)


  


#load the genes of interest
Genes_of_interest <- read.table("data/Genes_of_interest.txt", sep="\t", header=T, fill=TRUE, quote = "")
head(Arcog_mapping)


  





9.6.2 Make a vector to order our genes of interest

We use unique() to remove any duplicate gene names
arrange() can be used to order our dataframe by more than one column.

You notice here that the syntax for arrange() is a bit unusual and we use the %>% symbol (a so-called forward pipe operator). This symbol is commonly used in the dplyr and tidyr packages which are extremely useful to summarize data. This function passes the left hand side of the operator to the first argument of the right hand side of the operator. In the following example, the data frame Genes_of_interest gets passed to arrange()

#order metabolic genes
Genes_Metabolism_order_temp <- Genes_of_interest %>% arrange(Order, Order2)

#make a unique vector for our genes of interest
Genes_Metabolism_order <- as.character(unique(Genes_Metabolism_order_temp$Gene))

9.8 Make count tables

9.8.1 Generate a count table for our genomes of interest
Now we want to count, how often does a genome (i.e. NIOZ134_mb_b41_2) have a gene. I.e. how often do we want arCOG00570, arCOG01358, …

9.8.1.0.1 Do this via a loop (not executed, just an example)
Notice:
Since we run this chunk with , eval = FALSE we can still see the code but it is not executed. This is done because some computations take some time, which we do not want to spend, but I still want to show the code to give some alternative examples.

#count the number of proteins for each genome of interest
y <- c()
for (i in Bin_order) {
  x <-  table(subset(Input_long, BinID %in% paste(i))$gene)
  y <- cbind (y,x)
}

#clean-up the table
Counts_Table_loop <- y
colnames(Counts_Table_loop) <- Bin_order
Counts_Table_loop <- as.data.frame(Counts_Table_loop)
kable((head(Counts_Table_loop)), format='markdown')

#the '-' (=not identified genes) is also counted and listed in the first column and removed at this step
Counts_Table_loop <- Counts_Table_loop[-1,]
kable((head(Counts_Table_loop)), format='markdown')



9.8.1.0.2 Do this via ddply ((not executed, just an example))
New functions:

spread() = converts our long to a wide dataframe by using the BinIDs as new column names, the count table as values to populate our dataframe and with missing values we print a 0.


#count data and clean header
Counts_Table_long <- ddply(Input_long, .(BinID, gene), summarize, GeneCount = length(gene))
colnames(Counts_Table_long) <- c("BinID", "geneID", "count")
kable((head(Counts_Table_long)), format='markdown')

#transform to wide format, with fill = 0 instead of a NA we add a 0
Counts_Table_wide <- spread(Counts_Table_long, BinID, count, fill = 0 )

#view data
kable((head(Counts_Table_wide)), format='markdown')



9.8.1.0.3 Do this via tidyr (usually a bit faster than ddplyr, which is why we use this way)
Here, we use the %>% symbol again: In the following example, the a subset of the Input_long data (only 3 columns, not the whole dataframe) gets passed to count()
New functions:

count() = A function of the dplyr package. Here, we count the unique protein IDs grouped by BinID and gene (i.e. roughly equivalent to the columns we want to keep)

10.1 Search for patterns with grep and grepl
Oftentimes you may need to filter a data set based on a partial character string that is beyond the scope of comparison operators.
R provides such functions (grep and grepl) that match character patterns in specified vector. While both of these functions find patterns, they return different output types based on those patterns.
In our growth data, we only want to print measurements of our controls (i.e. the mock treatments). Our table has many rows, so we only look at the first few results with head().
#find the row index values with mock treatments using grep
head(grep("mock", growth_data$Condition))

[1] 1 2 3 4 5 6
To see how grepl works, let’s first try it on a short vector with our three conditions. Both strains (129E and 13C) contain a 1, the mock treatment does not:
#use grepl to search for conditions that contain a 1, returning FALSE/TRUE statements for each element
#with "TRUE" representing matched patterns
grepl("1", c("mock", "129E", "13C"))

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
On our dataframe, grepl gives one TRUE or FALSE for each of the 594 rows. Instead of printing them all, we can count the TRUE values with sum(), i.e. the number of plants treated with a strain:
#count the rows where the condition contains a 1
sum(grepl("1", growth_data$Condition))

[1] 385
Now lets use this to actually filter our data table for a pattern.

text:
grep returns numeric values that correspond to the indexed locations of the patterns
grepl returns a logical vector in which ‘TRUE’ represents a pattern match.

10.1.3 Discard matching rows

#view dataframe
head(filter_for_not_a_value)

[1] 2323    4

#check the dimensions of our new dataframe
dim(filter_for_not_a_value)

[1] 1167    4


Other comments:

Using regular expressions (programming symbol pattern) will increase their functionality
Specified patterns are case sensitive (‘t’ does not equal ‘T’)
Any matching pattern will be returned despite the context in which that pattern is located (i.e., grep(‘the’, data) with return matches for ‘the’, ‘theme’, ‘heather’, ‘breathe’, and so on. This is where regular expressions are useful for specifying where in a string the pattern should appear.



10.1.4 Using regular expressions
A regular expression (regex or regexp for short) is a special text string for describing a search pattern. You can think of regular expressions as wildcards on steroids. You are probably familiar with wildcard notations such as *.txt to find all text files in a file manager.
As an example, let’s grep the strains that have a number with 3 digits.
If you want to know more, see this cheat sheet here

filter_3digits <- growth_data[grepl("[0-9]{3}", growth_data$Condition),]

#check the structure of our data
head(filter_3digits)


  


#check the dimensions of the original dataframe
dim(growth_data)

[1] 594   5

#check the dimensions of our new dataframe
dim(filter_3digits)

[1] 210   5


Here, [0-9] searches for every number from 0-9 and with {3} we look for three numbers in a row. 129E matches, but 13C does not, because it only has two numbers.
